articles.title: Counting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Results are expected from 2.30am BST in the north London poll to choose a replacement for former PM Keir Starmer

A quick reminder of

blocks.text: Counting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Counting is currently under way in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in north London, where voters are choosing a replacement for former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
Starmer announced his decision to step down as an MP in September after being ousted from No 10 by Andy Burnham.
Camden council has said the result is expected to be called between 2:30-4am UK time.
We’ll bring you the latest developments as we get them.

blocks.caption: Ballots being counted after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in London on Thursday.  Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: Key events

items: 12m agoWho are the candidates?
18m agoCounting under way in Holborn and St Pancras byelection

blocks.text: Zack Polanski’s had a tricky week leading up to the byelection amid criticism he showed a lack of leadership over a policy equating Zionism with racism adopted at last weekend’s Green party conference
Polanski missed the vote on it in Brighton in order to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

But the Greens’ adoption of the policy has been highly contentious – drawing sharp rebukes from mainstream UK parties, British Jewish groups and Israel – while also prompting four of five Green MPs to publicly reject the move.

The motion said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. The head of the Jewish Greens condemned it and said she might leave the party, although it was supported by some Jewish Greens.

Even members who supported large parts of the motion were unhappy about its narrow conception of Zionism which some fear could brand those in favour of the idea of a Jewish homeland – but not specifically the modern-day state of Israel – as racist.
The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after their adoption of the policy drew dismay from the group representing European Greens.
Who are the candidates?
A quick reminder of the byelection candidates in Holborn and St Pancras:

items: Labour – Sagal Abdi-Wali
Green party – Zack Polanski
Conservative party – Ewan Cameron
Reform UK – Peter Newman
Liberal Democrats – Patrick Thomas Stillman
Restore Britain – Tyler Kurtis Johnson
Workers party – George Galloway
Rejoin EU – Briony Anne Lonbay Kapoor
Climate party – Clare Fischer
UK Voice – Ketankumar Pipaliya
Ukip – Ben Walker
Monster Raving Loony party – Barmy Brunch
Communist League – Jonathan Silberman
Christian Peoples Alliance – Helen Spiby-Vann
Independent – Tom Darwood

blocks.caption: Peter Walker

blocks.text: Peter Walker
Holborn and St Pancras is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold.

Keir Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Zack Polanski. In 2019 Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes.

Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat.

blocks.caption: Green leader Zack Polanski (second right) campaigning on the streets of Holborn and St Pancras last month. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

blocks.text: However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour.

Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies.

Polanski’s fortunes, in contrast, appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's arraignment on grave threats case postponed anew --lawyer
articles.summary: The Quezon City Regional Trial Court 98 on Friday postponed anew the arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte on grave threat charges.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 9:18am Updated October 9, 2026 9:25am
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court 98 on Friday postponed anew the arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte on grave threat charges.
"Minabuti nga ng judge na huwag munang ituloy ang arraignment today," Duterte's legal counsel Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim said in an ambush interview.
This would be the second postponement of the arraigment which was originally scheduled on September 11.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on August 11 filed three counts of grave threat charges against Duterte in connection with remarks she made in an online press conference in 2024.

During the press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
On September 4, Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court issued a warrant of arrest for Duterte over three counts of grave threats.
She posted bail on September 5.
Emerging from the Quezon City Hall of Justice, Duterte greeted her supporters and thanked them. She also thanked her lawyers for doing their job. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias forecast to bring dangerous storm surge, with millions under warnings in US
articles.summary:
Residents in areas from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Florida urged to ‘evacuate if told to do so’

Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings on…

blocks.text: Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings on Thursday as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of dangerous storm surge, hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding.

Isaias intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, and has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, as well as evacuation orders and school closures in several Florida counties as officials urge residents to prepare for its arrival.

The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Thursday evening that Isaias, now a category 2 hurricane, has sustained winds of 100mph (160km/h). It is expected to make landfall in the northern Gulf coast late Friday or early Saturday.

The NWS warned that Isaias was “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf coast on Friday” and that it was expected to bring a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast.

Storm surge warnings, issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas have been urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.
The NWS further warned that “preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds in the warning area should be rushed to completion today”.

Hurricane warnings were in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf county line in Florida, with the NWS warning that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi”. Residents were being urged to prepare for possible “long-duration power outages”.

Tropical storm warnings were in effect from parts of Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf county line to Aucilla River in Florida. Gusty winds were also possible across parts of the Yucatán peninsula on Thursday.

Isaias was expected to bring heavy rain to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, with 3-7in of rain expected from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region.
The NWS warned that localized rainfall totals of up to 15in were possible, and noted that flash and urban flooding was possible, along with isolated river flooding.

Isolated tornadoes could also develop on Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far south-western Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida”.

On Thursday afternoon, the Georgia governor, Brian Kemp, issued a state of emergency ahead of Isaias, for all 159 counties, enabling emergency management teams to “make necessary arrangements and position needed resources ahead of the storm’s impact”.

“As we always do with weather events, we’re hoping for the best but preparing for the worst,” Kemp said. “I encourage all Georgians to take this storm seriously and prepare now by stocking up on food, batteries, flashlights, water, and other necessities in case of severe weather impacting communities Friday night through Saturday.”

It came as Alabama governor, Kay Ivey, declared a state of emergency in 40 counties on Wednesday, saying the order would allow officials to take “any needed steps ahead of landfall”. A flood watch is also set to take effect for all of central Alabama from 7pm local time on Friday through 7am local time Saturday morning.
The Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, also declared a state of emergency this week for 25 counties.

At a news conference on Thursday afternoon, DeSantis said that the hurricane was “expected to make impacts with the winds as early as Friday afternoon” and said “landfall is projected at this point to be late Friday night into the wee hours of Saturday morning. It’s moving pretty quickly.”

He added: “Execute your plan now if you’re in that area, execute it, it’s something that we’re going to have to get through, we’re going to have impacts, and I’ve pretty much said that from the outset, there will be impacts.
“We are assuming that this could reach category 3 status.”

Several counties in Florida have issued local emergencies and evacuation orders. Officials in Okaloosa county declared a local state of emergency on Wednesday and ordered some residents in coastal areas to evacuate.

On Thursday, Florida’s Walton and Franklin counties issued mandatory evacuation orders for some areas. Officials in Escambia county issued an evacuation order for residents in areas including Perdido Key, Innerarity Point, Pensacola Beach and other low-lying areas.

DeSantis said on Thursday that the Florida division of emergency management was coordinating with all local counties to address resource requests and to position equipment before the storm. He also said that 900 personnel with the Florida department of transportation were conducting pre-storm preparations.
Several school districts in Alabama and Florida have announced closures, while Florida State University’s Tallahassee campus announced it will be closed on Friday.
The hurricane is also expected to disrupt travel. Destin-Fort Walton Beach airport said it would close all operations at 9pm local time on Thursday, and remain closed until further notice.
Meanwhile, Pensacola airport announced it would be closing to commercial operations at 10am CT on Friday, with the reopening date and time to be determined.

The Federal Aviation Administration warned on Thursday that “Hurricane Isaias may lead to oceanic route closures in the Gulf” and that thunderstorm delays are possible in Orlando, Tampa, Miami and Fort Lauderdale. The Southern Rail Commission said Amtrak’s Mardi Gras service along the Gulf coast will be suspended through the weekend.
Additionally, starting Friday, the Crescent service between New Orleans and Atlanta will be suspended until Monday.

In Tennessee, the NWS office in Morristown warned that “remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring heavy rain and strong, gusty winds to our area this weekend”. The office said that “high winds could top 60–70+ mph in the eastern TN mountains and foothills, with isolated flash flooding possible in heavy rainfall areas”.
In Ohio, the NWS office in Wilmington cautioned that Isaias would hit the Ohio valley this weekend, with strong winds expected, with possible “widespread rain” and storms.

In Pennsylvania, the NWS office in Pittsburgh said “moisture from Hurricane Isaias is forecast to reach our region this weekend” and that they were expecting “soaking rain, but risks of significant flooding are low”.

articles.title: Alberta premier unclear when asked to define threshold for questions 1 to 9 on referendum ballot
articles.summary: On Thursday, CBC News asked Premier Danielle Smith to define what she considers a strong mandate and what the thresholds will be for taking action on each question.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at a news conference in Edmonton on Oct. 8, 2026. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
On Thursday, CBC News asked Premier Danielle Smith to define what she considers a strong mandate and what the thresholds will be for taking action on each question.
Albertans can vote on 9 questions about immigration and constitutional issues on Oct. 19

Premier Danielle Smith was not clear on Thursday when asked what she considers a strong mandate to move forward on policies about immigration and constitutional issues after Albertans vote in this month’s provincial referendum.

On Oct. 19, Albertans can vote on five questions about immigration and four questions relating to Canada’s Constitution, along with a question added by the provincial government about separatism: whether to stay in Canada or hold a second binding referendum on separating from the country.

While Smith has said she considers 50 per cent plus one a threshold for the question about separatism, she demurred when asked by CBC News at an unrelated news conference on Thursday what she considers a strong mandate or a threshold for the other nine questions.
“I’m going to look at what the results are," she said. "We are very pleased that there’s a lot of interest in participating in this vote.

"We want to make sure that there’s a lot of feedback from Albertans. So we’ll look at the voter turnout and we’ll look at the results and we’ll be able to give you some clear direction on Oct. 20 once we’ve heard from Albertans."
Paperwork for a special mail-in ballot for Alberta’s 2026 referendum is shown. (Nate Luit/CBC)
Smith was pressed on why Albertans are not being given a clear definition of what the government considers a strong mandate before they cast their ballots.

“I think people know that I want these nine [proposals] to get an endorsement," she said. "I don’t want to prejudge the outcome, but I’ve made it pretty clear that I would like to proceed on these nine issues.
"We heard about it through the Alberta Next Panel, but I want to hear from Albertans to make sure that they agree that this is the right direction to go."

At an announcement on April 23 to unveil a new website for the government's fall referendum questions, Smith said her government wants "voters at the ballot box who have considered the facts carefully, and we want a strong mandate to deliver change for Albertans."
CBC News asked Smith why the province is not using the benchmark of 50 per cent plus one.
“Fifty per cent plus one is normally … what you would use, sure,” she said on Thursday as her press secretary cut off the CBC News reporter who was attempting to clarify her response.

The five questions about immigration relate to whether there should be increased provincial control over immigration, whether non-permanent residents should be prohibited from accessing provincially-funded programs, whether non-permanent residents should be restricted for at least 12 months before qualifying for provincially-funded social support programs, whether non-permanent residents should be charged a fee for health care and education and whether proof of citizenship should be required to vote in provincial elections.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know
A look at constitutional questions being asked in Alberta's referendum

blocks.text: The other questions ask Albertans whether they support amendments to the Constitution so provincial governments select justices, whether there is support to abolish the Senate, whether provinces should opt out of federal programs while keeping the federal funding associated with them and whether provincial laws should be prioritized over federal laws.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Julia Wong is a senior reporter based in Edmonton.

items: President Trump announced that the US will not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing productive discussions between the two countries.

The ongoing war has negatively impacted Trump's approval ratings and is a concern for Republicans ahead of the elections, with a significant portion of Americans disapproving of his handling of the situation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump said on Thursday, October 8, that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November’s US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having “productive” talks about ending the six-month-old war.

“We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”

The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November’s election.

Some 60% of Americans — including one in four Republicans — disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war.
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer.

Iran’s state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country’s Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make “meaningful” reductions in its enrichment capacity.
The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sydney festival 2027: 11 international dance works to headline ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ program
articles.summary: Making its southern hemisphere debut, Dance Reflections will feature collaborators of Rosalía, Madonna and Beyoncé – and a high-wire takeover of the Cutaway

blocks.text: A “once-in-a-lifetime” program of dance works of scale will be coming to Sydney in January, including 11 international works from France, Belgium, South Africa and beyond making their Australian premiere.

The program, which triples the scale of the dance offering at the last Sydney festival, will bring 174 performers and crew to Sydney, with the crowning jewel being the acclaimed French choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider. The 2024 work features 21 dancers from the Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève and four elite athletes, navigating a “cat’s cradle” of high wires and slack lines, to the mesmerising, minimalist music of the avant garde composer Julius Eastman.

Outsider will be performed in a purpose-built 720-seat theatre in the recently renovated Cutaway at Barangaroo – the first time the space has been activated for theatrical performance. The venue will also host Christos Papadopoulos’s My Fierce Ignorant Step; a double bill of works by the Chinese choreographer Tao Ye with his company TAO Dance Theatre; and a new work by genre-defying collective (La)Horde, best known for their work with pop stars such as Madonna, Sam Smith and Rosalía.

blocks.caption: Rambert in Hop(e)storm by (La)Horde, who will be bringing a new work to Sydney. Photograph: Hugo Glendinning

blocks.text: Under the banner of the Sydney festival, which announces its full program on 19 October, this is the first southern hemisphere outing for Dance Reflections, an international festival funded by French jewellery maison Van Cleef and Arpels, which has previously been staged in cities such as London, New York, Hong Kong and Seoul.

“Dance Reflections has been a real gamechanger in the creation and dissemination of dance on this scale,” says the Sydney festival director, Kris Nelson, who witnessed first-hand the impact the inaugural festival had in London, where he was working at the time.

In Sydney, he says, it will be a “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity for dance lovers, including the Australian debuts of Ouramdane, (La)Horde and the rising star Leïla Ka, who has choreographed for Beyoncé. The Belgian master Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker will return to Australia with her company Rosas, and, from Australia, there’s a brand new work from Indigenous and intercultural dance company Marrugeku.

blocks.caption: Marrugeku’s artistic directors Dalisa Pigram and Rachael Swain. The Indigenous and intercultural dance company will be premiering a new work at Dance Reflections. Photograph: Philip Thompson

blocks.text: It’s been more than a decade since Sydney’s last major dance festival, Spring Dance. Launched by the Sydney Opera House in 2009, it ran for four years and featured superstars such as Akram Khan and Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, before being dropped in 2013 for financial reasons. At the time, the Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron described the city’s dance audience as “relatively small but passionate”.

Nelson is hoping that’s changed. “I’m not daunted,” he says, pointing to the viral popularity of dance on TikTok, and the pop cultural work of choreographers such as (La)Horde and Leïla Ka, who draw from queer club culture and street dance.
after newsletter promotion

The festival is offering 10,000 A-Reserve tickets across the program at $49, and two works will be free: Trisha Brown’s seminal Roof Piece, in the gallery spaces of the Art Gallery of NSW; and the Belgian choreographer Cassiel Gaube’s tribute to house music, Soirée d’études, in the public space at Carriageworks.

“I’m really excited because we’re presenting a massive sampler of different kinds of dance, from the super classical to the acrobatic, to clubby and queer, personality-driven dance with big characters on stage, and works where you’re watching these incredible bodies do amazing geometry,” Nelson says. “This is your chance to test it out.”

articles.title: Jim Chalmers delays ATO’s controversial ban on credit card payments following business outcry
articles.summary:
Treasurer earmarks funds for year-long transition period for tax office, delaying ban’s 30 November start date

A controversial credit card ban for payments on tax bills will be delayed by…

blocks.text: A controversial ban on credit card payments on tax bills will be delayed by more than six months, after the federal government overruled the tax office and announced new stopgap funding.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced on Friday extra funding on Friday, after days of criticism and calls from small business to halt the ban.
The tax office will continue to accept credit card payments via third parties as well as other free and low-fee payment methods like debit card and bank transfers from July 2027.
The decision followed criticism of the ATO’s response to the Reserve Bank’s moves to ban credit card surcharges, something the federal government sought to take credit for.
The tax commissioner, Rob Heferen, announced moves in early October to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from 1 December.
He said continuing to accept card payments would cost the ATO almost $200m a year, as those costs can no longer be passed on to card users.

But some business owners, particularly smaller operators, use credit card payments as a cashflow tool, managing their liabilities by using credit when required. Estimates suggest about 5% of small businesses use credit card payments for tax bills.
Because tax liabilities are legislated by federal parliament, the ATO said it could not build card payment costs into charges paid by taxpayers.
Government ministers had sought to pressure the ATO into changing its position this week, amid strong criticism from the Coalition and business lobby groups.
The ATO is an independent authority and the government cannot direct the tax commissioner’s decisions.
“We’ve stepped in to ensure that the tax office can take credit card payments until the end of June next year,” Chalmers said on Friday.

“This will give them the time to consult more with small business and to get it right, this recognises the really important contribution that small businesses make to our local communities and to our economy more broadly.

“Now we try not to interfere with the RBA or the ATO when they go about designing and implementing this surcharge ban, but it’s really important that we have stepped in today to make it possible for the ATO to continue to take credit card payments until the end of the financial year.”
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, said this week that small businesses needed the credit card facility in place.
“They’ve got to manage cash flow. What they are looking for is for one clear, consistent approach and solution from government.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte appears in QC court for grave threats arraignment
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte appeared before a Quezon City court on Friday, October 9, for her arraignment on three counts of grave threats.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case on Oct. 9, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte appeared before a Quezon City court on Friday for her arraignment on three counts of grave threats.
The proceedings were scheduled for 8:30 a.m. before Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court.

During an arraignment, the charges are formally read to the accused, who is then asked to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty for each count. If Duterte pleads not guilty, the case will proceed to trial.

The court initially scheduled the arraignment for September 11 but deferred it after granting a motion from Duterte’s camp. The court ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to comment on the motion before resolving it.

Duterte’s lawyers have questioned the trial court’s jurisdiction over the case, arguing that the Constitution grants impeachable officials limited procedural immunity while in office. The court had earlier rejected her bid to dismiss the charges on jurisdictional grounds.
The DOJ filed the three counts of grave threats on August 11 over Duterte’s remarks during an online press conference in November 2024.

During the briefing, Duterte said she had spoken to someone about killing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
The charges were filed under Republic Act 10175, or the Cybercrime Prevention Act. Duterte has denied the allegations.
On September 4, the Quezon City RTC issued an arrest warrant against Duterte after finding probable cause to hold her for trial. The court set bail at P120,000 for each count.
Duterte posted bail on September 5, paying a total of P360,000 for the three charges.
The case will be heard as Duterte faces an impeachment trial before the Senate. The alleged threats against Marcos also form part of one of the Articles of Impeachment against the vice president.

articles.title: U.S. ICE agents shoot and wound man during arrest in New York City
articles.summary: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in New York City while making an arrest, officials say.

image.caption: A car surrounded by police tape at the scene of a shooting Thursday in Manhattan. (Seth Weni/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in New York City while making an arrest, officials say.
Mayor says he will talk to president and demand ICE enforcement ends in his city

U.S. federal immigration agents shot and wounded a Dominican man while arresting him in New York City on Thursday, in what the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) called a "targeted enforcement operation."
Protesters said it was an example of the dangers of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The man survived and is being treated at a hospital, DHS said. It did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer "discharged his weapon" during the incident and the man was injured.

The department described the man as a "criminal illegal alien" with a prior grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. He was arrested in December 2023 but was released, DHS said, blaming "reckless" policies in Democrat-led cities such as New York.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for an end to all ICE raids in the city in a statement on social media. Demonstrators at the scene chanted, "ICE off our streets now!"
A person holds a sign near the scene of the shooting. (Seth Wenig/The Associated Press)

An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene "to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security," but offered no other details. Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities.
The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx.
Difficult to identify ICE agents, resident says

Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with DHS branding.
Witnesses, he said, were screaming.
Neighbourhood resident Alfred Silva, 38, called for federal officers to more clearly identify themselves, saying one was wearing a construction safety vest and carrying a rifle.
"We need to have better transparency to understand who we're dealing with, because anybody in the street can just put on a vest and pull out a gun and claim to be ICE," Silva said.
"I feel like regardless if you're left or right, we should understand that this shouldn't be happening."
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting.
"We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why," she said.

Videos and photos posted by bystanders on social media show a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back in the immediate aftermath of the shooting.

Another video shows New York City police officers picking up an apparently injured man and carrying him into a police vehicle. Nearby, a damaged car blocking the roadway is seen with small holes in two of its windows.

articles.summary: The shooting happened in the afternoon in the Bronx, with details still emerging. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the incident and urged Donald Trump to end ICE actions in the city.

image.caption: New York leaders are calling for answers and action following the shooting as protests erupt Image: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: A man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent during an arrest, New York City metropolitan police said Thursday.
What do we know so far?
The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. local time (2100 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, which is one of New York's five boroughs.
Details are still emerging, but the New York Police Department has denied that its personnel were involved in the shooting.
"The individual who was shot is at a nearby hospital and is currently conscious and receiving medical attention," the NYPD said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump's administration has scaled up ICE raids in major US cities to detain and deport people who are in the US illegally.
Local media in New York said ICE was involved in the latest shooting in the Bronx, which has sparked protests.

blocks.caption: People at the scene of the shooting expressed their dismay with federal immigration raids in New York CityImage: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: Mamdani says he is contacting Trump to end ICE actions in NYC
New York City Zohran Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he is calling President Trump.

"This is an unconscionable and incredible serious situation," Mamdani said in a post on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agent terrorize our communities.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul earlier said she has been briefed on the incident.
"We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding the incident," Hochul said in a statement posted on X.
"New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why."
The Department of Homeland Security is the parent agency of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). DHS has not yet publicly commented on the incident.
ICE, CBP fatal shootings raise alarm in second Trump term
Deadly ICE and Border Patrol shootings have drawn major controversy during Trump's second term, particularly regarding the training and oversight of the agents.
An ICE agent killed a 37-year-old US citizen, Renee Good, during their operations in Minnepolis in January, triggering demonstrations there and in several other US cities.
Later that month, Alex Pretti, another US citizen, was killed by two US Customs and Border Protection officers agents in Minneapolis following an altercation.

articles.title: B.C. teen rescued from 'Widowmaker' mountain trail says AI isn't to blame
articles.summary: Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route.

image.caption: Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called 'the Widowmaker' climbing route. The Vancouver teen is pictured here on a hike in September 2026. (Joelle Gowryluk)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday after accidentally taking what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route.
Bryce Gowryluk, 16, was lifted from Crown Mountain by helicopter Saturday
A B.C. teen making global headlines after being rescued from the side of a mountain says AI is not the reason he became stranded.

Bryce Gowryluk, 16, an experienced hiker from Vancouver, is frustrated by this week's news stories claiming he used Anthropic's AI chatbot, Claude, to plan the alpine scramble that ended in a helicopter extraction from what's called "the Widowmaker" climbing route on Crown Mountain.
"People are really taking it out of context, because people think that I planned … or was coerced by the AI to go on the Widowmaker, which is not true," Gowryluk told CBC News.
"I just feel like people who are judging the situation are really unfair in their stance."

Volunteer rescue organization North Shore Rescue posted on Facebook Sunday that they responded to a call the day before about a hiker stranded on Crown Mountain, at the base of the final, vertical climbing wall of the route known as the Widowmaker.
They eventually located him by helicopter. A rescue tech belayed down to the hiker and moved him to "a suitable extraction point," and they airlifted him out.
The harrowing photos, and a rescuer's comments that the teen used AI to plan his route, quickly went viral.
A photo posted by North Shore Rescue on Sunday shows a teen who had to be rescued from the side of Crown Mountain, north of Vancouver, the day before. (North Shore Rescue/Facebook)

Gowryluk says he spent three days planning what was meant to be about the eight-hour hike Saturday from the top of Grouse Mountain to Crown Mountain and back. He consulted AllTrails and Google Maps, and admits he cross-referenced some information about the terrain using Claude, but says he mostly used the AI agent to help him with his packing list.

He left home around 7:30 a.m., took the bus to Grouse Mountain, rode the gondola to the top and walked to the alpine trailhead. His route was meant to eventually take him through a rugged scramble, but instead he mistakenly turned onto an unmarked route called the "Widowmaker Arete."
"There's no warnings," he said.

At first, he says, the terrain was "nothing too extreme," so he assumed he was on the right path — until it became too steep and too smooth to count as a scramble at all. Going back down, backwards, wasn't an option, and neither was staying still on the rock face, he said.
"That's when I realized something has gone terribly wrong," Gowryluk said, but he kept climbing, focused on putting his hands and feet wherever they would fit.
"I knew that fear would just lead me to panic, and panic would lead me to my death."
He finally made his way to a ledge wide enough to stand on and called his mom.
LISTEN | Rescuer recalls getting to teen stranded on mountain:
As It Happens6:32Rescuer cautions against 'blindly following' AI directions after chatbot leads teen hiker astray
'I think I made a wrong turn'
Joelle Gowryluk says her phone rang in the early afternoon.

Bryce is an air cadet with survivalist training and is a certified belayer, she said, and so Joelle felt her son was well prepared for yet another hike — especially in a busy area like Grouse on a sunny, clear day.
But when she answered the phone and asked what was going on, Bryce said, "I think I made a wrong turn," Joelle said.
"He wasn't frantic. He just said, 'Mom, I have to call the North Shore Rescue. I can't go any further. I've climbed too high and I can't get back down.'"

North Shore Rescue search manager Paul Markey said they were dispatched by the police to rescue Gowryluk, who he described as "an adventurous sort." And regardless of whether it was via chatbot or his own navigation, Markey says Gowryluk found himself on a significantly challenging alpine climbing route without the proper equipment.
"He was perched on a ledge," Markey told CBC Radio's As it Happens.
"He was very scared, as would [be] anybody in that particular position."

They flew to him quickly, Markey said, and hoisted two rescuers down to him from the helicopter. Then they got him to an area where he could safely be hoisted back up, and brought him back down to the base of the mountain.
"It was definitely, a really try-not-to-freak out experience," Gowryluk said, recalling dangling from the helicopter by a harness.
A still image taken from a video provided by Bryce Gowryluk of Vancouver shows the helicopter that rescued him from Crown Mountain on Saturday. (Bryce Gowryluk)
Experts warn about relying on AI
Bryce came home that day "pretty shocked," Joelle Gowryluk recalled. Typically, he returns from the mountains very happy and very tired, she said, "but a good tired."

Climbing is positive for his mental health, she added, saying she'll continue to encourage him to hike and climb safely — and always with another person — and hopes other teens will consider it, too. But she worries about the media attention that she feels has focused on Bryce's use of AI while downplaying his experience.
"He's no stranger to these North Shore mountains," she said.
When CBC asked Bryce Gowryluk when he might head back for another mountain hike, he replied, "probably Saturday."

items: Maritime experts urge use of verified weather reports after kayaker capsizes in B.C. waters
Rescues in the Rockies cost millions each year. Who pays for them?

blocks.text: While the hiker and rescuer give different reports for how AI was involved in Gowryluk's ill-fated trip, it's just one recent example where chatbots were involved in people finding themselves in dangerous situations.
In September, for instance, maritime first responders warned people not to rely on AI for weather reports after rescuing a man whose kayak capsized on B.C.'s south coast.
He had tried to use an AI chatbot to determine the safest time to paddle.

Markey says the North Shore Rescue probably gets about 150 calls per year, but that Gowryluk's was the first call they'd ever had about someone potentially led into a dangerous area by AI. He's worried it will just be the first of many, he added, and cautioned climbers from "blindly following" a route suggested by artificial intelligence.
"Claude has never been onto that mountain," Markey said.
Bryce Gowryluk, now 16, is pictured hiking as a child. Bryce is an experienced hiker, an air cadet with survivalist training and a certified belayer. (Joelle Gowryluk)

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. articles.title: Ombudsman vows to protect IP rights after suspending Puerto Princesa exec
articles.summary: In a statement on October 7, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla cited the agency's decision finding Carlo Benitez Gomez, Department Head II of the Puerto Princesa City Environment and Natural Resources…

blocks.text: Office of the Ombudsman along Agham Road in Quezon City.
Wikipedia / patrickroque01

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman reaffirmed its commitment to safeguard the rights of indigenous cultural communities against unlawful and improper government operations, following a ruling that penalized a Puerto Princesa City environmental official for bypassing required indigenous clearances in a river dredging project.

In a statement on October 7, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla cited the agency's decision finding Carlo Benitez Gomez, Department Head II of the Puerto Princesa City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO), administratively liable for Conduct Unbecoming of a Public Officer.
Gomez was meted a penalty of one-year suspension without pay.
Should the suspension no longer be enforceable due to separation from service, the penalty will be converted into a fine equivalent to six months of his salary.

The case stemmed from a complaint filed by the leadership of Sambayaang Tagbanua kat Barangay Simpokan Inc. (STBSI), representing part-owners of an ancestral domain belonging to the Tagbanua Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) in Brgy. Simpokan, Puerto Princesa City.
In 2022, local barangay officials passed a resolution for the rehabilitation and dredging of the Malinao River to mitigate flooding following Typhoon Odette.

Serving as technical secretariat of the City Mining Regulatory Board (CMRB), Gomez issued a clearance to proceed with the project, which allowed the rehabilitation contractor to receive 6,000 cubic meters of surplus gravel extracted from the river to offset operational costs.

STBSI strongly opposed the project, citing a lack of proper consultation, the desecration of their ancestral waters, and a direct violation of Section 59 of Republic Act No. 8371, or the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (IPRA) of 1997.

In its decision, the Ombudsman held that Gomez issued the project clearance prior to obtaining the required Certification Precondition from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and without waiting for final approval from the CMRB.

“Gomez's act of issuing clearance to proceed without the required certification precondition from the NCIP and without waiting for the CMRB's approval is a deliberate transgression of rules or procedures as provided under the IPRA,” the Ombudsman’s ruling read.

“Gomez failed to observe professionalism and justness and sincerity so as to discourage wrong perception of his role as a dispenser or peddler of undue patronage. Such conduct or behavior is considered unbecoming of a public officer,” it added.

Meanwhile, participating barangay officials — including the former Barangay Captain, seven councilors, and the Sangguniang Kabataan chairman — were cleared of administrative liability, as their involvement was limited to passing a resolution regarding the river's overflow.

Remulla issued a warning to public officials to strictly adhere to laws protecting indigenous rights, emphasizing that the anti-graft watchdog will continue to act against illegal and unjust acts affecting IP communities.

articles.title: Plans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government intervention
articles.summary:
State planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local council

Plans for a grand new public square in centre of Sydney are in doubt after the…

blocks.text: Plans for a grand new public square in centre of Sydney are in doubt after the New South Wales planning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney.

The lord mayor, Clover Moore, released renders in August for the plaza opposite Sydney’s town hall. The design for the space, which the council had expected to be completed by 2031, include a semi-circular clearing projecting eastwards towards Hyde park, with a fountain and a grove of native trees.

blocks.caption: Artists render of the proposed Sydney Town Square redevelopment. Illustration: JPW and ASPECT Studios

blocks.text: The plans have been the source of a battle between Moore and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, who has said he does not support the project, describing it as “too expensive, majorly disruptive for Sydney”, and said it would close down businesses in the area. It had also become a flashpoint in a culture war, ridiculed in the Sydney tabloid The Daily Telegraph, which published AI-generated images of the new square heaving with protesters.

The council began finalising discussions with the owners of the last of seven buildings needed to be acquired and bulldozed for the project in recent months. The demolition and construction was expected to cost $150m.

But on Friday, the planning minister, Paul Scully announced he had declared the project a state significant development (SSD), after seeking advice from the NSW Independent Planning Commission, taking the decision for approval away from the council.

“This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application,” he said.
They have also been opposed by Woolworths, whose town hall location occupies one of the buildings that would be demolished under the plans.

Scully said the IPC would make the determination on any proposal submitted by the City of Sydney. Under the SSD pathway, the planning minister himself is the consent authority, unless the IPC is delegated to take on that role.
In a surprise statement on Friday, Moore welcomed the decision to declare the project state significant, saying, “I could not agree more”.
“Regardless of who assesses it, we remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported.”

“The City owns the buildings, has responsibly saved the money over a 40 year period to deliver the project debt-free, and has had some of the world’s leading designers and architects work on the plans.”

“This has, however, been an unusual intervention. The government generally takes planning decisions away from councils to speed up development, not slow it down, and in this case it stepped in before a development application even existed.”
More details to come.

articles.title: Barricades installed around QC court ahead of Sara Duterte arraignment
articles.summary: Steel barricades were installed around the Quezon City Hall of Justice Friday morning ahead of Vice President Sara Duterte's scheduled arraignment on a grave threat case.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 7:54am
Steel barricades were installed around the Quezon City Hall of Justice Friday morning ahead of Vice President Sara Duterte's scheduled arraignment on a grave threat case.
The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) placed the railings to enforce rules prohibiting protests within a 200-meter radius of court buildings.
“Yun po ay security assistance po natin as requested by the Office of Judiciary Marshals,” QCPD spokesperson Police Major Jennifer Ganaban said in an interview on GMA News’ Unang Balita.
(That's our security assistance as requested by the Office of Judiciary Marshals.)

“And according na rin po sa ating Supreme Court rule na ang protesters po, pickets, and rallies are prohibited within 200 meter-radius of the Supreme Court Hall of Justice, or any other building housing a court sala in the Philippines,” she added.

(And according to our Supreme Court rule that protesters, pickets, and rallies are prohibited within 200 meter-radius of the Supreme Court Hall of Justice, or any other building housing a court room in the Philippines.)
So far, authorities have not monitored any planned protests or received requests for permits for gatherings near the courthouse.
However, the QCPD still deployed Civil Disturbance Management personnel in case protesters arrived.
Ganaban clarified that Duterte's supporters were not being prevented from expressing their views but were being directed to follow existing rules to ensure public safety and orderly activities.

During the previous scheduled arraignment on September 11, supporters who sought permission to hold a protest near the courthouse were directed to Freedom Park at Quezon Memorial Circle after their permit request was not approved, according to the police.
Ganaban pointed out the need to protect courts from external pressure, intimidation, or other forms of influence.
The QCPD was also taking the necessary measures to ensure the safety of Duterte and everyone present at the courthouse, according to Ganaban.
Arraignment
Duterte's arraignment is scheduled at 8:30 a.m. on Friday. It was rescheduled from September 11 after the court granted her camp's request for postponement.
Her camp has questioned the RTC's jurisdiction over the case before the Supreme Court and had sought a temporary restraining order.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on August 11 filed three counts of grave threat charges against Duterte in connection with remarks she made in an online press conference in 2024.

During the press conference, Duterte said she had already talked to someone to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then House Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.
On September 4, Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court issued a warrant of arrest for Duterte over three counts of grave threats.
She posted bail on September 5. —Joviland Rita/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: US to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution: Pentagon
articles.summary: US Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth had said that Nidal Hasan would be executed by firing squad and that it would be done "in public." Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961.

image.caption: Hegseth said he would 'make sure that people are able to watch' Hasan's execution [FILE: September 30, 2026]Image: Alex Wong/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.
The confirmation came a day after US Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth had said Hasan's execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in "public."
Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.
What did Pete Hegseth say about Nidal Hasan's execution?

In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said Wednesday that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
Hegseth was speaking to right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which ended a nearly 10-month deployment on Thursday.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth said.
Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and will be the first to be done by firing squad since World War II.
Hegseth added: "I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win."
What do we know about the Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan?
US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.
A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.
The announcement that Hasan will be executed by firing squad comes amid the fallout of the botched execution of Christa Pike.

items: The barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections have been postponed to 2028, leaving 73,731 seats vacant since the 2023 elections due to resignations, deaths, removals, or absences.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao has the highest vacancy rate at 46.54%, with most empty seats being from SK councils, which make up 77.21% of the total vacancies.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) were again postponed to 2028. What happens to the thousands of seats that have been vacant since the 2023 elections?

According to data from the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), there are 73,731 seats vacant as of September 29. The officials who filled these seats were elected in 2023 but have either resigned, died, been removed from office, or been absent without leave during their term.
Now, nearly 9% of the 840,200 barangay and SK positions nationwide are empty. They will remain so for two more years, unless local chief executives appoint new officials to fill the gaps.

But such appointments would again deprive voters of their right to choose their public officials. That means millions of Filipinos — especially in regions where the concentration of empty seats is relatively high — will either be left without elected barangay and SK officials or have no say in who leads them.
Here’s a map showing which regions have the most vacancies.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has the most vacancies, with nearly half or 46.54% of all its barangay and SK seats empty.

The region has had a long and bloody history of electoral violence. The Peace Research Institute Frankfurt said such incidents were particularly prevalent at the barangay level. Even before it became the BARMM in 2019, it was standard practice in the region to “negotiate” the elections as a way to avert violence stemming from heated political rivalries between clans, according to a 2013 VERA Files report.
The BARMM has low literacy rates, too, which the Asian Network for Free Elections said remain a challenge for voter education and knowledge of the electoral process at large.
Behind BARMM in most vacancies is the Zamboanga Peninsula, with 21.08% of seats empty, and Cordillera Administrative Region at 18.23%.

Most of the empty seats are from the SK councils, making up 77.21% of the 73,731 vacancies. The percentages of vacancies within each position also show that positions lower than the SK chairperson usually reported the most empty seats in these youth councils.
And with the polls postponed to 2028, these numbers can only be expected to grow.

“If they’re not planning to serve as public officials for the rest of their lives, and they see their SK term as just a stepping stone to another section of their career, then most probably we’ll see a good number of SK officials retiring,” Ona Caritos, executive director of election watchdog Legal Network for Truthful Elections, told Rappler.
“Because two years is two years — it’s not 6 months…. It’s a long time for a young person or a young individual to wait and delay his life plans yet again just for the barangay.”
While vacancies in barangay positions are always filled by way of succession or mayoral appointment, empty SK seats can be handled in three different ways.

Special elections are the preferred mode of filling these vacancies. But a 2024 DILG circular says officers-in-charge can also be appointed by the mayor, or they can be elected during a Katipunan ng Kabataan (KK) Assembly, which is a gathering of all registered youth voters in a barangay.

But past attempts at special elections have often been deferred or suspended usually due to funding problems. Appointments are also frowned upon because they take away the voters’ opportunity to choose their own leaders.

An election during a KK Assembly is the remaining alternative. But these assemblies have long been criticized for failing to convene even when past laws had required them to meet at a frequency of four times a year.
The SK Reform Act only requires the assembly to meet at least once every six months, though it can be called earlier by the SK chairperson or through a written petition.
As a result, issues in filling these vacant seats have also been present in previous BSKEs.

The DILG does not have data on how long the seats for the current batch of officials have been vacant, Jhona Cabading of the DILG’s National Barangay Operations Office told Rappler. But the recent BSKE postponement only stands to make the issue of these vacancies worse. – Rappler.com

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer addresses suicide attempts in strike group after record deployment – live
articles.summary: Captain Dan Keeler says there were ‘no lost lives on board’ and adds that deployment was ‘first experience with combat’ for most sailors
articles.byline: Robert Mackey (now); Uwa Ede-Osifo, Shrai Popat, Maya Yang and Tom Ambrose (earlier)

blocks.text: USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer addresses suicide attempts in strike group

In a brief news conference on Thursday afternoon, Captain Dan Keeler, the USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, addressed widespread reports of mental health challenges faced by his crew during their long deployment.

“For most of my sailors, that this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” Keeler said. “I understand the anxiety that that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience, and the great majority responded like sailors always do - with honor, courage, and commitment.”

“They are fantastic, fantastic sailors and marines, and they’re going to be cared for continuously on the next coming few months,” he added. “I deployed with five chaplains and a very well staffed mental health team. We got our sailors any care they needed and got them back in the fight when it was appropriate.”

blocks.caption: Captain Dan Keeler, the USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, met family members after the returned to San Diego following an extended deployment to launch strikes on Iran. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters

blocks.text: Near the end of the news conference one reporter asked: “Were there some sailors who did try to commit suicide or jump overboard?”
“The key number that I like to focus on is zero; there were no suicides on board. There were no lost lives on on board,” Keeler replied.

“The suicide attempt number,” he went on. “You know, the secretary of the navy put out a number that encompassed the entirety of the strike group,” Keeler said, referring to a letter to Congress from acting navy secretary Hung Cao last month in which he wrote that there had been a total of eight suicide attempts across all the ships in the strike group led by the Lincoln.

“I think that key point has been lost when he, the secretary of the navy, put out the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, that encompasses several thousand more sailors than what’s on board behind me,” Keeler added.

“We want the suicide attempt number to be zero. Having done this many, many times with the demographics that I have on board and the, you know, the stressful mission that we conduct, that’s unrealistic,” he continued. “That’s why I go to sea with a very, very well staffed mental health team. And when we had acute mental health cases, they immediately get seen by that mental health team and evaluated.”

blocks.text: Sam Levine
Eric Leventhal knows he’s going to vote for a Democrat in Congress when he goes to the polls in Missouri this November – the problem is he has no idea which candidate is going to be on his ballot.

In the state’s August primary, he voted for Fred Wellman, a Democrat running in the state’s second congressional district. But after a long and complicated legal battle sparked by Donald Trump’s desire to gain every advantage in the upcoming midterm contest, the districts have changed for the general election that will determine which party controls Congress. Leventhal said he lived right near the border of the first and second congressional district, so now he’s not sure which one he’s in.
“It is dizzying and embarrassing, frankly,” said Leventhal, a 35-year-old stay-at-home father.

Leventhal’s experience crystallized the mix of anger and confusion felt in Missouri, where an effort by Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map devolved into a saga that seemed to have as many twists and turns as the gerrymandered districts themselves.

articles.title: 'Drunken intent is still intent': Crown argues Cody Chubey guilty of murder
articles.summary: Lawyers made closing arguments on Thursday at the trial of Cody Chubey, who is charged with first-degree murder in the death of Danielle Dobersheck on March 10, 2024, in Melfort, Sask.

image.caption: Crown prosecutor Jennifer Souter, centre, speaks with Danielle Dobersheck's family and supporters outside Melfort Court of King's Bench. (Hannah Spray/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Lawyers made closing arguments on Thursday at the trial of Cody Chubey, who is charged with first-degree murder in the death of Danielle Dobersheck on March 10, 2024, in Melfort, Sask.
Judge to give decision in 1st-degree murder trial in December
Warning: This story contains graphic details of a murder scene.
While the defence says the ability to form intent while intoxicated is the key issue at a Melfort murder trial, the Crown says drunken intent is still intent.
Cody Chubey is charged with first-degree murder of Danielle Dobersheck, his long-term partner. He beat her to death in a motel room on March 10, 2024. She was 30 years old and a mother of three.
The lawyers made their closing arguments on Thursday in Melfort Court of King's Bench.
Defence lawyer Peter Abrametz said repeatedly that Chubey, 38, accepts responsibility for killing Dobersheck, but argued he should be found guilty of manslaughter, not murder.
Chubey testified on Wednesday that he had no memory of killing her because he was blacked out from drinking alcohol.
Abrametz said the way Chubey reacted when police arrived at the scene showed he had no consciousness of guilt. He was calm and said he had gotten into an argument with his girlfriend.
Cody Chubey arrives at Melfort Court of King's Bench on Oct. 7, 2026, to testify in his own defence at his first-degree murder trial. (Hannah Spray/CBC)

Court heard Chubey was sitting in a motel room where the walls were covered in blood. Dobersheck was dead in the bathroom, along with the bloody snow shovel that Chubey used at the end of the assault.
"We respectfully submit that … there was no intent to cause death," Abrametz said.
Evidence shows intent, Crown argues
Case law has established that "drunken intent is still intent," Crown prosecutor Jennifer Souter argued.
Regardless, no evidence was presented about how much Chubey had to drink that night, other than his claim that he blacked out, Souter noted, calling his testimony not credible or reliable.

"That said, if the court accepts the accused's testimony that he has no memory of the incident, the Crown says that the accused is confounding an inability to form memory with Mr. Chubey not forming a specific intent to commit murder," Souter said.
"The two concepts are not synonymous."
She argued the evidence showed that Chubey intended to kill Dobersheck.
Danielle Dobersheck died on March 10, 2024, in Melfort. (Danielle Dobersheck/Facebook)
Souter cited an audio recording played in court, made by the couple staying in the room next door, that captured the sounds of Chubey beating Dobersheck.
In it, Chubey accused Dobersheck of cheating on him and demanded she tell him who it was with. He repeatedly said, "I'll kill you," while she tearfully denied cheating on him and screamed for help.
Souter also argued that Chubey killed Dobersheck while unlawfully confining her in the motel room. A homicide committed during an unlawful confinement elevates the crime to first-degree murder.
She cited testimony from the man in the room next door, who said he heard Chubey tell Dobersheck she wasn't going to go to the hospital, but that she should go to the bathroom and clean herself up.

items: Danielle Dobersheck faced threats, violence before homicide, say friends, family

blocks.text: Then, the man heard Chubey get angry again, after he couldn't find his phone. He said he heard banging from where the bathroom was.
When police arrived, they found the locked bathroom door had been kicked in.

Souter cited testimony from the motel owner that the door wasn't damaged before that night, and from a police officer who said a bloody footprint on the door was likely from someone doing a "donkey kick" with their back to the door, to force it open.

Souter argued there are two pathways to a conviction of first-degree murder on the issue of unlawful confinement — if the judge finds Dobersheck couldn't leave the motel room due to Chubey's control of her, or if he finds that she was seeking refuge in the bathroom.
Justice Sean Sinclair said he would need some time to consider the arguments.
His decision is scheduled for Dec. 11.
