Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
articles.summary: A new film paints the Meta founder as a villain. But the tech firm seems immune to bad publicity, writes our North America tech correspondent.

blocks.text: Image source, CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images / CTMG, Inc./Leah Gal
ByLily Jamali
North America Technology correspondent

blocks.caption: Lily Jamali

blocks.text: Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it

blocks.text: Image source, Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty Images
This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it

His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.

But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.

And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.

Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning

blocks.text: Image source, CTMG, Inc./Leah Gallo
Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning

In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.

And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.

Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users. Outside one case in California this summer, protesters highlighted the names of young people they say died as a result of social media harms. Meta disputes many of the claims

blocks.text: Image source, Godofredo A. VÁSQUEZ / AFP via Getty Images

Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users. Outside one case in California this summer, protesters highlighted the names of young people they say died as a result of social media harms. Meta disputes many of the claims
To some, the trust issue feels existential
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.
"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."
'Withstanding the blowback'

But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.

And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.

One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company.
"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.
However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust.

Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time).

It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet.
But Muse works best when users hand over some of their most personal information to the company, including credit card information, purchase histories and access to email inboxes.

It's a big ask for a company whose reputation on privacy has been sullied, starting a decade ago with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which followed the revelation that the data of millions of Facebook users was breached and used by a political consulting firm.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zuckerberg launched Facebook in 2004, aged 19, while studying at Harvard University

blocks.text: Image source, Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty Images
Zuckerberg launched Facebook in 2004, aged 19, while studying at Harvard University

Just two days after Zuckerberg's keynote at Meta Connect, another New Mexico jury found Meta lied about how Facebook used personal information. (The company has said it disagrees with the verdict and will defend itself against what it says are efforts to distort its record.)
So are customers willing to hand over that data for the convenience of using Muse?

Some users say yes. Since its launch one month ago, Muse already has more than five million downloads and more than three million weekly active users - outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT when that was first introduced, in the North American market.
Zuckerberg has laid out a vision in which Muse couples with an ever-expanding line-up of Meta AI smart glasses, enabling users to summon hands-free what he calls "personal superintelligence".

Meta clearly has big plans for its smart glasses. "I think they're making an investment to position themselves as a category leader," says Kate Winick, principal analyst at Forrester, covering social media and influencers. "However big this category turns out to be, they will own it - for now."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zuckerberg attended President Trump's inauguration ceremony last year, along with Elon Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Zuckerberg attended President Trump's inauguration ceremony last year, along with Elon Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

The glasses are divisive, and have been labelled by some as "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film covertly. The company has moved to stop users from tampering with the light that indicates a photo or video is being captured. Zuckerberg also just announced new audio-only smart glasses, an apparent bid to quell privacy concerns.
But the company's most strident critics remain wary.

"Consumers know that Meta has problems, and that to date we haven't been able to trust them to make their products safe for children. So why would a consumer want to trust them with some of their most private and sensitive information?" says Brooke Istook of the Heat Initiative, a campaign group.
Privacy versus convenience
In his speech, Zuckerberg briefly addressed the sensitive issue of privacy. At one point during his talk, an image flashed on the screen behind him of its Muse mascot embracing a blue padlock.
"Given how personal Muse and the content on your glasses is, we designed state-of-the-art privacy and security into all these systems from the beginning," Zuckerberg told the audience.

He touted a personal virtual machine, for example - essentially a self-contained computer system running inside Meta's cloud, where it says Muse users' data will be stored. Zuckerberg promised it would keep every customer's information secure, and that soon "even Meta won't be able to see that information". He said the virtual machine will be launched later this year, with further privacy protections coming.

Meta's focus on privacy and security seems aimed at reassuring consumers. But Winick says users still have to opt into many of those protections. "I think if they thought they could get away with not doing that, they would," she says.

Not long after Zuckerberg took the stage in California, social media users started reporting cases of Muse running amok, including claims that the agent read emails without permission. Meta has pushed back against these reports, saying it does not believe that Muse accesses emails unless a user has consented.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Campaigners celebrated in Los Angeles earlier this year after hearing that a US jury found Meta and YouTube liable in a social media addiction trial

blocks.text: Image source, Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty Images
Campaigners celebrated in Los Angeles earlier this year after hearing that a US jury found Meta and YouTube liable in a social media addiction trial

In the end, the bulk of users may be willing to make some concessions on privacy if it means convenience and utility, says Moorhead. "If the consumer sees the trade-off as beneficial, then they'll keep it going," he says. "This is why Facebook and Instagram still have billions of users."

On the financial front, the social media advertising business – its cash cow – routinely brings in significant revenue. Meta reported $60.8bn in revenue and $15.9bn in profit for the second quarter of this year.
Consistent profits have helped fuel bets from the much-mocked Metaverse, to its current mass expansion of AI infrastructure.
And on Muse? "It's a very real time-saving benefit that a lot of people will want and will like," says Winick.
AI investment is not cheap. Meta has now taken on $83.7bn in long-term debt, according to its most recent financial statement.

Still, Meta executives are bullish about the company's pivot to AI. "It's really about your agent, who can do work on your behalf, who is your constant ally in whatever you're trying to accomplish in your goals in your life," Andrew Bosworth, the company's chief technology officer, said in an interview with the BBC.
Meta has big plans. But its future may ultimately depend on whether its users can trust it.
Top image credit: CTMG, Inc./Leah Gallo

articles.title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire breaks silence to BBC
articles.summary: Vitalii Zhykovych gives his own account of the attempted assassination of Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev.

blocks.text: A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.

Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.

He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.

Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.
Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko.

articles.title: 1st of 29 monarch butterflies tagged on Canadian Prairies reaches Mexico after perilous migration
articles.summary: The first of more than two dozen endangered monarch butterflies tagged with radio trackers on the Prairies this summer has made it to Mexico to overwinter, a mere five weeks after fluttering off from…

image.caption: A monarch butterfly sips nectar from a meadow blazing star flower on Aug. 26 at the Living Prairie Museum in Winnipeg, one of several hot spots for the endangered species this summer. The first of the 29 butterflies tagged with radio trackers there in August made it to Mexico earlier this week. (Bry

blocks.text: Manitoba

The first of more than two dozen endangered monarch butterflies tagged with radio trackers on the Prairies this summer has made it to Mexico to overwinter, a mere five weeks after fluttering off from Winnipeg.
Journey continues for most of the butterflies tagged in Winnipeg this summer, but some aren't going to make it

The first of more than two dozen endangered monarch butterflies tagged with toothpick-sized radio trackers this summer has made it to Mexico to overwinter, a mere five weeks after fluttering off from Winnipeg.

A butterfly with the decidedly sciency-sounding moniker "MB26011" accomplished the physical feat Tuesday, when she crossed the northern Mexico border, dodging predators and vehicle collisions during the perilous five-week migration.
"She's done about 2,300 kilometres in about 40 days. It's really incredible," said Laura Burns, the conservation program manager at the Assiniboine Park Zoo in Winnipeg.
"I think it's one of the most incredible migration stories in the animal kingdom. That's why people are so enamoured with monarchs, because it's a truly remarkable feat that they accomplish."

Laura Burns, conservation programs manager at the Assiniboine Park Zoo, sits on a butterfly bench at the zoo's pollinator garden on Thursday. She hopes the data researchers glean from the trackers helps them identify key stopover spots so they can better protect those areas. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

Burns worked along with Environment and Climate Change Canada researchers and staff at the Living Prairie Museum — a tall-grass prairie preserve in Winnipeg — to tag 29 monarch butterflies there from Aug. 26-27.
The Manitoba effort, spearheaded by Environment Canada, marked the first time monarchs were tagged west of Ontario.

As they bopped from flower to flower over two days, the team nabbed the butterflies with nets and then — very gingerly — pinned them down, dabbed them with eyelash glue, stuck the solar-powered radio tags on and set them free.

Conservation researchers and members of the public have been tracking their movements on the Project Monarch app ever since. The trackers ping as the monarchs fly by radio telemetry towers between Canada and Mexico.
1st monarch butterfly tagged on Canadian Prairies makes it to Mexico
At least three of the 29 Manitoba monarchs appear not to have made it out of the province. Their tags fell off or otherwise stopped sending signals.

Those casualties may tell researchers something about the myriad threats the delicate butterflies face. Monarchs were listed as endangered in Canada a few years ago under the federal Species at Risk Act, largely due to habitat destruction associated with agriculture and other human activity.

items: These endangered monarchs are booming in wet, hot prairie summer

blocks.text: Several other butterflies still on the wing appear to show just how gritty the showy creatures can be.
For MB26011 to make it into Mexico, she would've also had to have gotten a little lucky.
"Not only is it a really far distance, and she needs the energy to fly that far, the weather would've had to have been on her side as well," said Burns.

"Then you factor in other conservation concerns like big agricultural fields or cities, cars, predators.... It's really remarkable not only that she went so far, but that she managed to navigate all of those obstacles."
A monarch caterpillar chows down on swamp milkweed leaves at the Living Prairie Museum in August. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

While MB26011 has made it across two borders already, she still has a few hundred kilometres to go until she reaches the oyamel fir forests in central Mexico, where she'll meet up with scores more of her kind.

Once there, she'll have a few good bacchanalian months breeding with the rest, then die. Come spring, the next generations will do the pilgrimage she did in reverse, and arrive back on the Canadian Prairies.
But that long winter resting, suckling on sweet flowers and mating isn't yet guaranteed for the rest of the Manitoba 29.

Data from Project Monarch and Environment and Climate Change Canada shows the migration path of two of the 29 butterflies tagged in Manitoba — Eddie, who was southwest of Kansas City as of Thursday, and MB26011, who made it to Mexico on Tuesday. (CBC News Graphics)
Eddie, one of the butterflies CBC News documented being tagged and released in August, was just southwest of Kansas City as of Thursday. He has another 1,700 kilometres or more to go.

Burns hopes the data gleaned from the trackers helps Canadian researchers identify key stopover spots along the migration pathway, so that they can collaborate with experts in other jurisdictions to better protect those areas moving forward.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.

articles.title: No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real
articles.summary:
Peter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illness

  • Full report |

blocks.text: Eighteen months ago, in an off-the-cuff remark during a discussion on disability benefit cuts, Wes Streeting said mental health conditions were being “overdiagnosed”, riding headlong into another culture war.

He later apologised for the comment, but at the time it seemed the then health secretary had endorsed a populist view that ordinary stresses and disappointments had become too often medicalised, resulting in a surge of bogus clinical diagnoses and creating a “snowflake generation” of fragile, avoidant and workshy young people.

Prof Peter Fonagy’s mammoth review of mental health conditions, autism and ADHD in England, commissioned by Streeting nine months ago, has no truck with the snowflake generation caricature: the steep rise in the prevalence of mental health problems such as anxiety and depression is real, he says, and so is the distress and difficulties they can cause.
double quotation markI am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced

The review says the drivers of this rise are cultural and social. Young people are exposed to Covid disruption, financial and housing insecurity, and competitive school and social stresses that are exacerbated by social media. Support services, from Sure Start to youth clubs, have been swept away. There is less belonging, it says, and more loneliness.

Fonagy himself was a severely depressed teenager in 1960s London, he reveals in an unexpectedly tender foreword to the review. Today’s youth have it much harder, he writes. “I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced. They are not fragile. They are outnumbered.”

Sceptics may yearn for a mythical time when troubled young people just had to pull their socks up, fit in and learn to deal with life’s inevitable hard knocks. Fonagy makes clear the past is another country and you cannot rewind the clock. “Simple answers are rarely adequate,” he writes.

Fonagy’s brief was not explicitly to settle culture war disputes, however, and the review warns that the rising prevalence of mental illness, ADHD and autism has wider consequences: public services are overwhelmed, people suffer because they cannot get care or support, and the cost to the taxpayer is unsustainable.

The review is frustrated by the public debate’s focus on whether there is too much or too little diagnosis. There is a risk of overdiagnosis, Fonagy admits (though he says there is no evidence it is happening at scale), and he is scathing about the growth and reliability of unregulated private providers of diagnostic assessments.

But the deeper problem, the review argues, is the disproportionate power of the diagnosis in accessing clinical care, special educational needs support in schools, or disability benefits. That encourages unfairness: those who can afford private diagnosis have a higher chance of getting support.

Fonagy’s solution is to reduce the heavy reliance on diagnosis (NHS diagnosis waiting times are 64 weeks). An individual’s needs should be identified and triaged early with the goal of ensuring they swiftly get the support they need.

The challenges Fonagy identifies are also those being grappled with by the imminent Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, the Timms review of disability benefits, and the government’s Send changes. His solutions may not fly, but his warning is clear: “Continuing as we are is not sustainable.”

articles.title: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?
articles.summary:
Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’

  • Full report |
articles.byline: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent

blocks.text: The Fonagy review of NHS England’s mental health, ADHD and autism services was commissioned in 2025 by Wes Streeting, then the health secretary, in response to growing concerns that spiralling waiting lists for assessment, diagnosis and care threatened the NHS’s ability to meet the demand.
The 607-page report, published on Friday, says that without a radical overhaul, mental health and neurodiversity services will be overwhelmed. Here are some of its key findings and recommendations.

items: 1. Unprecedented and growing levels of distress are realThe report is categoric that mental distress has “increased substantially across the population”, is real and affects everyday functioning, and that the rise “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”. About one in four 16- to 24-year-olds are now thought to have a common mental disorder such as anxiety and depression, up from one in six in 1993, while self-harm, eating disorders, OCD, PTSD and drug dependence have also increased.About 4 million children are in “serious distress”, and if current trends continue that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report says. At current rates self-harm cases could reach 2.5 million across England’s population. But rates of severe mental illness such as bipolar or schizophrenia have remained much more stable, while hazardous drinking has declined.Chart of numbers of cases of mental health need

2. The system is failing everyoneWith the cost of mental ill health standing at £300bn a year, “continuing as we are is not sustainable,” the report warns. “Not for the people waiting weeks, months or years, becoming more distressed because help is locked behind waiting for a diagnosis; not for those with the most severe needs who cannot access specialist care; and not for a society paying the human and economic price of failing to support people to participate in family, community, education and working life.”

3. Overdiagnosis of ADHD and autism is not yet widespread but is a growing riskWhile the proportion of the population thought to have ADHD and to be autistic has remained broadly stable at an estimated 3.8% and 1.2% respectively, the recent exponential rise in those diagnosed, as well as even larger numbers waiting to be assessed, means we have reached a tipping point where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with ADHD and autism, said Prof Simon Wessely, the review’s vice-chair.The report finds that the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years, and for 12- to 17-year-olds more than 15-fold, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively. And with more than 560,000 people waiting for an ADHD assessment and more than 254,000 for an autism assessment, the proportion of people with a diagnosis of ADHD or autism is expected to rise further.ADHD diagnoses chartAutism diagnoses chart“This does not, by itself, establish that overdiagnosis is currently occurring at scale,” the report states. “However, the evidence suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery.”

4. Private companies should be banned from advertising ADHD and autism assessmentsThe report finds that NHS spending on independent-sector ADHD services rose by 252% over three years and that private providers accounted for more than a third of NHS-funded autism assessments in the 2025-26 financial year. Responding to the report’s call for greater regulation, the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said the government would “make all diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism Care Quality Commission-regulated, so people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”.Chart of self-reported cases of autism, ADHD or other neurodivergenceShe stopped short of committing to banning private-sector advertising of ADHD and autism assessments to the public, instead saying the Advertising Standards Authority would be asked to review it, “to ensure people receive accurate information and are not exploited by companies encouraging them to seek assessments they may not need”.

5. The NHS should provide a needs-first serviceProf Peter Fonagy, the review’s chair, said the NHS needed to shift from a diagnostic labelling model to a flexible, needs-led system. “Diagnosis remains essential and must be protected,” he said, but added: “What has to change is that it is no longer the only door through which help can be reached.”Instead, people should be able to seek help through school, GP or community services, mental health services, social care, employers and family hubs. Support should be given at the point of need, not contingent on a diagnosis. And there should be a single service for mental health and neurodevelopmental support to provide more joined-up help.In response, the Department of Health and Social Care committed to a major overhaul of services to ensure “earlier, needs-led support for children, young people and adults, without long waits for clinical diagnosis”.

6. Scrap first-come-first-served waiting listsPatients waiting for a diagnosis should be prioritised. Rather than a first-come-first-served system, mental health and neurodiversity services should ensure those with the highest needs – such as self-harm, multiple difficulties or risk of imminent school exclusion or unemployment – get specialist assessment sooner.Waiting lists should be “actively reviewed” to enable that prioritisation. But the authors denied that would leave those with less acute symptoms without any route to diagnosis, stressing: “No one should be removed from a pathway without appropriate assessment, communication and discussion.”

articles.title: NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds
articles.summary:
England-focused mental health review returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system

  • Explainer |

blocks.text: The NHS in England is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.
The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.

It found there was an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and urged ministers to toughen the regulation of the private clinics to which many people are turning because they cannot get assessed quickly by the NHS.
The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.
The review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.

The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.
The evidence shows that sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles, the 607-page report found.

“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.

The report’s conclusions may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.

Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London, dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes” who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.

He lamented that an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”

The explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity has left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms, Fonagy said. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than were doing so in 2019. Another 254,000 people were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total number waiting to more than 800,000. Almost all – 90% – had been waiting for at least three months.

The number of six- to 11-year-olds being diagnosed with autism has also soared. It jumped 20-fold to 4.58% between 2000 and 2025 and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years, from 0.1% to 4.06% – a 40-fold jump. And the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years and more than 15-fold in 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively.

While 4 million children already suffer from “high psychological distress’’, if current trends continue, that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report warned. The number of under-18s who self-harm could also rise from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.
The exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition, Wessely warned.

The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.

The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.
after newsletter promotion

The 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.
Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.

Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61% of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57% had ADHD symptoms.
The report said their needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.
The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health backed Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who received care.

“Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime,” said Dr Ronny Cheung, its officer for health services.
The NHS moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations in putting together the forthcoming mental health strategy, which is due by the end of the year.

In her response, she promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care. She has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.
She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”
She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated but did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.

articles.title: Over 60 Pinoy fishermen detained in Sabah over alleged illegal fishing
articles.summary: The crew members allegedly failed to present valid identification documents and work permits, and were accused of violating immigration laws and Malaysia’s Fisheries Act of 1985.

blocks.text: Satellite rendering shows Sabah, Malaysia
Google Earth / Philstar.com's screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — At least 65 crew members of a Filipino fishing vessel are detained in Sabah, Malaysia, after being nabbed by the Malaysian coast guard for alleged unauthorized fishing.

The Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) confirmed in a social media statement released September 30 that it seized the Filipino vessel and its crew members during a routine patrol on September 27.
The fishing vessel was reportedly found 18 nautical miles west of Mantanani Island at around 1:30 p.m.

Several Malaysian media outlets reported that four tonnes of sea produce suspected to be worth around 350,000 Malaysian ringgits, or at least P5 million, were found in the vessel upon initial inspection.
The crew members allegedly failed to present valid identification documents and work permits and were accused of violating immigration laws and Malaysia’s Fisheries Act of 1985.

Based on Paragraph 15 of the mentioned law, fishing or attempting to fish is prohibited in Malaysian fisheries waters unless there is an international fishery agreement between the government of Malaysia and the government of the country where the vessel came from.

Paragraph 56, meanwhile, provides that any fish found in foreign vessels are presumed to have been caught in Malaysian fisheries waters, while any fishing equipment are presumed to have been used for fishing in their waters.

Currently, Malaysia and the Philippines have no existing bilateral agreements for commercial fishing. Both countries are signatories to a multilateral agreement with Indonesia covering the Sulu-Celebes Sea.
Appeal for help

According to a report from Batangas-based news outfit Balisong Channel, a family member of one of the detained fishermen from Nasugbu, Batangas, is appealing for the government’s help in monitoring the case.
They called on the Department of Foreign Affairs and other concerned agencies to ensure the safety and welfare of the Filipino fishermen detained in the foreign country.
They also asked for help in monitoring and understanding the case.
Malaysia’s fisheries law allows authorities to initially detain arrested individuals for alleged violations. The arrested person is then subject to investigation.

However, if the probe cannot be completed within 24 hours, the authorities must bring the arrested individuals before a Magistrate or a judge, who can authorize continued detention for not more than 15 days while the probe is ongoing.
The continued detention does not mean the arrested individuals were already found guilty.

articles.title: Ex-German Chancellor Schröder attends Putin's birthday bash
articles.summary: Former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder still maintains a friendship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Tensions are high between Germany and Russia as the invasion of Ukraine continues.

image.caption: Putin has earlier called for Schröder to mediate talks between Russia and Ukraine Image: Pressestelle des Kremls

blocks.text: Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder attended Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday party, the Kremlin said Thursday.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands.
Schröder was visiting Hyperglobus branch after joining board
Schröder, who is 82 years old, was in Moscow visiting one of the branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain. The ex-German chancellor was named to the chain's supervisory board last week.

blocks.caption: Schröder was visiting a branch of Russian retailer Hyperglobus on Wednesday, the same day as Putin's birthday celebration Image: RBC/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hyperglobus was originally part of German retail company Globus Holding, which operates the Globus supermarkets in Germany and the Czech Republic.
Globus Holding also had supermarkets in Russia, but divested its stake last year, with those stores thus being spun off into seperate company Hyperglobus.
What backlash has Schröder faced in Germany over his Russia ties?
Schröder, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), served as Germany's chancellor from 1998 to 2005.
Since leaving the chancellery, Schröder has worked for Russian state-owned energy firms and has also maintained personal contact with Putin.
Why Putin turned to ex‑German chancellor as a peace broker
Schröder's fondness for Russia has drawn controversy, particularly since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, and he has also faced calls by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.
Schröder, however, has survived the attempt to be kicked out of his party.

articles.title: Curtis Flowers, US man wrongfully imprisoned for 22 years, dies aged 56
articles.summary:
Flowers, tried six times over 1996 murders of four people, faced execution before supreme court tossed his conviction

Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and…

blocks.text: Curtis Flowers, a Black man who spent more than 22 years in prison and was on death row in Mississippi before the US supreme court threw out his conviction and death sentence, has died. He was 56.
Flowers’ family confirmed that he died on Wednesday at his home in Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told the Associated Press on Thursday.
No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers’ legal team.
Flowers was 26 when he was arrested several months after the July 1996 shooting deaths of four people inside a furniture store in Winona, Mississippi.

At the time, prosecutors described him as a disgruntled former employee who sought revenge against the store’s owner because she fired him and withheld most of his pay to cover the cost of merchandise he damaged. Nearly $300 was found missing after the killings.
Flowers was tried in the killings six times. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the high court’s 7-2 decision in 2019 that the removal of Black prospective jurors deprived Flowers of a fair trial.

During the sixth trial in 2010, Flowers was sentenced to death. There were 11 white jurors and one Black juror who considered the case after district attorney Doug Evans struck five Black prospective jurors.
Flowers remained in prison for six months after the supreme court ruling because he was still under indictment. He finally was released in December 2019 after a judge set bond.
Mississippi dropped charges against Flowers in September 2020.

“Today, I am finally free from the injustice that left me locked in a box for nearly 23 years,” Flowers said in a statement. “I’ve been asked if I ever thought this day would come. I have been blessed with a family that never gave up on me and with them by my side, I knew it would.”

The individual was conscious and taken to a hospital, the NYPD said in a brief statement.
The NYPD has not specified which federal agency carried out the shooting, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Thursday evening.
The shooting took place at around 4pm in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx. The NYPD said they were not on the scene at the time of the shooting.

Witness video appeared to show several agents in the middle of the street in the aftermath, with one armed and another restraining a man on the ground, the New York Times reported. The City Reporter, a local news outlet, said video showed chaos after the shooting, with a crowd gathered and NYPD officers appearing to carry a man into the back of a vehicle.

Kathy Hochul, New York’s Democratic governor, said in a short statement that she had been briefed on the shooting, writing: “We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why.”

articles.title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.summary: "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it," the US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday.

blocks.text: A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the Second World War.

While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated.
The US government did not carry out executions for 17 years before the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions.

Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety".

articles.title: UK: Two Latvian men arrested for breaking into RAF base
articles.summary: The men were arrested for breaching a perimeter fence at a UK air base that houses US and NATO intelligence operations. The incident comes after an alleged terror plot at another air base in England…

image.caption: RAF Molesworth houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion CenterImage: Reuters

blocks.text: Two Latvian men have been arrested for breaching the perimeter fence at an RAF base used by the US military, UK police said Thursday.
The two UK residents, aged 36 and 32, were arrested by counterterrorism police at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in southeastern England, 70 miles north of London.
Police said they were being held on suspicion of trespassing, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK."
A former World War II airbase, RAF Molesworth, is now a non-flying facility that is managed by the US Air Force.
It houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Center, which provides information to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.
The incident comes after several men were arrested amid an alleged terror plot at another UK air base last month.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What do we know about the incident at RAF Molesworth?

According to a statement from Counter Terrorism Policing London, officers from the Ministry of Defense Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary began investigating an incident at approximately 10 p.m. local time on Wednesday after an abandoned vehicle was found near the edge of the base.
Police later discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence and arrested the two suspects at around 2 a.m. on Thursday.

The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage. They were later arrested on charges of entering a prohibited place with the intent to harm the UK.
Both men remain in police custody. Due to the nature of the offense, the matter is being investigated by counterterrorism police.
Is this related to the RAF Fairford incident?

On September 27, authorities discovered three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford, a British air base from which US bombers launched strikes against Iran. This triggered a widespread investigation that led to seven arrests.
Last weekend, the US Air Force brought home all the bombers deployed to the base.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the counterterrorism unit, said that while UK authorities are "very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites", there is "nothing to suggest" the incident at RAF Molesworth is related to what happened at RAF Fairford last week, although she added that the investigation was still in its "very early stages."
The US European Command acknowledged the incident but declined to comment on specific force protection measures.
Trump says RAF Fairford suspects known to US authorities

articles.title: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public."

image.caption: People kneel at the front gate to Fort Hood following a shooting rampage on the grounds Nov. 7, 2009 in Killeen, Texas. The execution by firing squad of the man convicted in the shooting will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public."
Nidal Malik Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people at the military base in 2009
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.
Hasan, a former U.S. army officer, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.
Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.
When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
Former U.S. major Nidal Hasan, the army psychiatrist convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, will be executed Dec. 3. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Getty Images)

Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.
Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting.
Trump approved the execution
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.
The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.

items: U.S. army moves to execute man convicted in 2009 deadly Fort Hood rampage by firing squad
Fort Hood massacre trial a rare U.S. military execution case

blocks.text: Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.

The military hasn't executed a servicemember by firing squad since the Second World War. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was executed by hanging.

articles.title: Toronto-area man sentenced to 68 months in prison for smuggling cocaine allegedly tied to Ryan Wedding
articles.summary: A Toronto-area man who pleaded guilty to smuggling cocaine for a drug network allegedly tied to former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding has been sentenced to 68 months — just over five and a…

image.caption: Rakhim Ibragimov, right, pleaded guilty for intent to distribute 375 kilograms of cocaine for a drug network allegedly tied to former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, left. (FBI/U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California)

blocks.text: Toronto

A Toronto-area man who pleaded guilty to smuggling cocaine for a drug network allegedly tied to former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding has been sentenced to 68 months — just over five and a half years — in U.S. prison.
Rakhim Ibragimov pleaded guilty for intent to distribute 375 kg of cocaine earlier this year

Uzbekistan-born Rakhim Ibragimov, known to associates as the “Russian” or “George,” pleaded guilty to intending to distribute 375 kilograms of cocaine “for the purpose of transporting it to Canada,” according to a plea agreement filed in June in California's central district federal court.
U.S. federal Judge Sherilyn Peace Garnett handed him his sentence Wednesday.

items: Toronto man to plead guilty to conspiring to smuggle cocaine for drug network allegedly tied to Ryan Wedding

blocks.text: The sentence includes three years of supervised release with conditions that include periodic drug testing and substance abuse counseling, according to the court records.
U.S. authorities caught Ibragimov in 2024
An agreed statement of facts laid out in Ibragimov's plea deal said he was caught by U.S. authorities in April 2024 after he traveled from Canada to California to oversee a drug shipment.
He was detained and then allowed to return to Ontario before being arrested again in October 2024 by Toronto police.

His arrest came around the same time that U.S authorities moved in on more than a dozen of Wedding’s alleged co-conspirators in Canada, the U.S., Mexico and Colombia for charges that ranged from drug trafficking to murder.
At the time of those arrests, Wedding was still at large. He was arrested earlier this year after a decade on the run.
What we know about Ryan Wedding's alleged Canadian associates
Ibragimov's plea deal did not make mention of Wedding, but his name is listed in an indictment document that includes Wedding and more than a dozen other alleged co-conspirators.

Around a year after his arrest, Ibragimov agreed to be extradited and face his charges in the U.S. Prior to his extradition, he spent around a year at Toronto South Detention Centre, his court records show.

His lawyer, Humberto Diaz, requested that his sentence be reduced to two and a half years given the time he spent at Toronto South, according to a supplemental sentencing filing presented to court. That filing also argued he is entitled to a reduced sentence given his "mitigating role" in the offence.
CBC has reached out to Diaz for comment.

articles.title: Hegseth says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be a public event
articles.summary:
Officials clarified execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, army psychiatrist who killed 13 people, will be livestreamed

Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army…

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. Officials later clarified the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow, the Associated Press reported.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad would carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.

“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.

Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.

In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.

But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.

The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in his second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five states in the United States allow for firing squads – Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah.

Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.
Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

articles.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate after offensive social media posts
articles.summary: Joachim Agou has been dropped as the B.C. Conservative candidate for Victoria-Beacon Hill. Party leader Lorne Doerkson said that "there is no excuse for this" after offensive social media posts came…

image.caption: Joachim Agou has been removed as the B.C. Conservative candidate for Victoria-Beacon Hill after offensive social media posts came to light. He refused to answer questions from reporters on Thursday. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Joachim Agou has been dropped as the B.C. Conservative candidate for Victoria-Beacon Hill. Party leader Lorne Doerkson said that "there is no excuse for this" after offensive social media posts came to light. The B.C. NDP had called for Agou to be fired over "absolutely horrific racism."
Joachim Agou would not answer questions from reporters on Thursday
The B.C. Conservatives have dropped Joachim Agou as the party's candidate for the Victoria-Beacon Hill riding after offensive social media posts.

In a social media post from from Sept. 7, 2025, that showed video of a car ramming into a group of pro-Palestinian protesters in Switzerland, Agou is seen in a screenshot commenting, "He should have reversed too!!!"
In November 2024, Agou also shared a meme that showed U.S. President Donald Trump, Elon Musk and right-wing European leaders that said "Make the west great again."
He also shared a meme on June 26, 2025 that showed Trump looking out from Air Force One.
It read "'Trump: My God, Pakistan looks like a shithole.' 'That's London Mr. President.'"
One of the controversial social media posts shared by Joachim Agou. (X)
The posts have since been deleted.
Agou refused to answer questions from reporters for several minutes on Thursday. He was set to meet with Victoria residents during a meet-and-greet at a café on Victoria's Fort Street.
The candidate would not say if he posted the tweets, if he subsequently deleted the tweets, if he would resign or if he regretted the comments.
He passed by the coffee shop without stopping, and walked several blocks to his car before driving away.
B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson dropped Agou as a candidate a little more than an hour after reporters asked him about the social media posts. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
Asked about the posts during an 11 a.m. news conference in Surrey, B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson initially said he wasn't aware of the posts.

When a CBC reporter read the posts in detail, Doerkson said he "of course" disagreed with the comments and promised to look into the candidate the "second I leave this podium." An hour and a half later, Agou was removed as a candidate.

"There is no excuse for this. I will not tolerate it. The candidate in Victoria-Beacon Hill is no longer a Conservative candidate. If elected, he will not serve in the [caucus]," Doerkson said in a statement.

items: How to watch the B.C. provincial election leaders' debate on Oct. 14

blocks.text: The B.C. NDP candidate for Surrey City Centre, Amna Shah, had called for Agou to be fired for the "absolutely horrific racism" in the posts.
Shah slammed Agou for "attacking the Pakistani community as 'a sh*thole,' joking about killing protestors, celebrating white supremacist figures."
This is the first time the B.C. Conservatives have had to remove a candidate during this campaign.

In Agou's bio, which has since been deleted from the B.C. Conservative website, he's described as a "test and evaluation engineer in the defence sector [who] runs a Victoria engineering consulting and media company."
It's unclear if Agou will run as an Independent candidate.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Katie DeRosa is the provincial affairs reporter for CBC British Columbia. She is based in Victoria. You can contact her at katie.derosa@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Official languages commissioner rebukes Air Canada CEO over English-only message
articles.summary: The commissioner of official languages of Canada is rebuking Air Canada's outgoing CEO for a condolence message he delivered almost entirely in English after a deadly plane crash in New York earlier…

image.caption: Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada Kelly Burke said the number of complaints over the video message shows that Canadians care about the use of both official languages in times of crisis. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The commissioner of official languages of Canada is rebuking Air Canada's outgoing CEO for a condolence message he delivered almost entirely in English after a deadly plane crash in New York earlier this year.
Commissioner received over 2,000 complaints about the video
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 08, 2026 5:19 PM EDT | Last Updated: 10 minutes ago
The commissioner's annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words — "bonjour" and "merci."

"The intensity of the reactions and the high volume of complaints received in response to this video show that both of our official languages genuinely matter to the Canadian public and that we must continue to protect them," Kelly Burke told reporters in Ottawa, adding that the complaints are still under investigation.
"This situation illustrates that bilingualism is an essential skill for any leader, whether in politics, federal public service or even in the private sector."

Rousseau's video message came after an Air Canada regional jet that took off in Montreal collided with a fire truck crossing the runway at LaGuardia Airport in New York on March 22, killing two pilots and sending more than 40 people to hospital.

items: Air traffic controllers allegedly left work early before fatal Air Canada crash at LaGuardia
A timeline of the Air Canada collision at LaGuardia airport that killed 2 pilots

blocks.text: Quebecer Antoine Forest and Mackenzie Gunther, from Ontario, were the two pilots killed in the collision.
Burke's report says it's important for Canadians to hear and see their leaders speaking equally in both official languages in times of crisis, "and not solely through an interpreter or subtitles."

Seven days after Air Canada posted Rousseau's video, the company's board of directors announced that he would retire by the end of the third quarter of 2026 and that it was considering a number of criteria for his successor, including the ability to communicate in French.
The commissioner's office said in an email that it received 2,425 complaints on the video, including 98 that arrived after the end of the current financial year on March 31.

items: Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau to retire later this year following language controversy
Air Canada CEO regrets inability to speak French following fatal plane crash
Air Canada names Anko Van der Werff as new CEO following predecessor's French-language fracas

blocks.text: Burke's 31-page report also touched on a number of other issues, including concern over how federal budget cuts could impact the government's language obligations and minority language communities.
"In the past, spending on official languages-related activities has often been targeted during periods of fiscal restraint," the report read.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to cut the size of the public service, relying mainly on attrition.

Burke said it's still too soon to measure the impacts of the 2025 federal budget, which laid out a plan to save tens of billions of dollars over five years in budget cuts and government efficiency measures.

"We're watching the government's actions closely on this subject, and we're waiting to see how the cutbacks will actually play out within the administration, so we can then assess how the government has addressed the concerns we raised at the beginning," Burke said.
Carney 'very disappointed' by Air Canada CEO's English-only message

The report also cited what it saw as positive developments, including $150 million in additional funding announced for CBC/Radio-Canada in the 2025-26 fiscal year and a Supreme Court decision in June that ruled New Brunswick's lieutenant-governor must be bilingual.
This decision "represents a step forward for the province's language rights and a major victory for official language minority communities," the report read.
The report also dedicated several pages to the use of artificial intelligence.
It noted that AI has potential to be used as a tool for translation and interpretation, as well as promoting bilingualism and language learning.
But Burke noted that AI is prone to errors, and has a "language bias" toward English due to the predominance of English-language "content and perspectives" on the internet.

The commissioner recommended that the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat incorporate official languages to its artificial intelligence strategy and other documents by March 2027, "so that they are systematically taken into account during the development, implementation and use of any tools, training, programs, policies or guidelines aimed at deploying artificial intelligence across the public service."

articles.title: DOJ alarmed over 6 million Filipinos using fake PWD IDs
articles.summary: There are about six million Filipinos who are using fake PWD (Persons with Disability) IDs and the Department of Justice (DOJ) find the figure alarming, according to the report of Darlene Cay on…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 5:05am

There are about six million Filipinos who are using fake PWD (Persons with Disability) IDs and the Department of Justice (DOJ) find the figure alarming, according to the report of Darlene Cay on "Saksi" Thursday.

"That's very alarming, tapos nagagalit tayo bakit daw dishonest ang mga... laging general rule, dishonest ang mga government official. Baka naman tayo bilang lahi, dishonest din," said Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida.
(That's very alarming, then we get angry because they say that government officials are dishonest... as a general rule, government officials are dishonest. Maybe we, as a race, are also dishonest.)
There are only 2.8 million persons with disability, based on the data from the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA).
However, there 8.5 million who have a PWD ID.
Vida said that using a fake PWD ID in every P1,200 bill in a restaurant, the government loses P50 in taxes while the restaurant owner loses P120 in income.
The NCDA is asking the help of the Justice Department.

"Ang nakuha kasi naming sentiment with the letter coming from the NCDA, is that the restaurant owners they feel parang at a loss na. Tapos na ang usapan, hindi na sila makagalaw. This is actually, telling them na "no" hindi pa tapos," said Dennis Arvan Chan, chief state counsel.

(The sentiment we got with the letter coming from the NCDA, is that the restaurant owners they feel like they are at a loss. The conversation is over, they can't move. This is actually, telling them that "no" it's not over yet.)
The new system, in which the PWD ID will be very pliable or can be checked whether it is legitimate or fake, could take three years.
For now, if a restaurant has doubts whether a PWD ID presented by a customer is fake or not they can get the information of the customer and check if they have a record with the LGU.
Chan said the restaurant owner can verify the validity of the ID but this can only be done after the discount has been given.
But the restaurant owner can file a case against the owner of the fake PWD ID for falsification of documents, and estafa.
"This might empower them more to take a more pro-active stand," said Chan.
The doctor and social worker can also be charged for issuing a fake PWD ID.
"Dahil sa panloloko mo, may nabibigatan," said Vida.
(Because of your deceit, someone is being burdened.)
"Ang panawagan ng Secretary of Justice, let's live honest lives. Ito po, manifestation po tayo kung sino po tayo bilang isang lahi," he added.
(The Secretary of Justice's call, let's live honest lives. This is a manifestation of who we are as a race.) — BAP, GMA News
