articles.title: Men accused of shooting Australian surfer brothers and US friend dead in Mexico to learn fate as trial concludes
articles.summary:
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, will address the court before a Mexican judge hands down the verdict

A Mexican judge is expected to hand down his verdict Thursday in the…

blocks.text: A Mexican judge is expected to hand down his verdict on Thursday in the high-profile murder trial of three men accused of killing two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in an alleged robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. The prosecution is seeking 150 years in prison for each of the accused.
The prosecution and defence were expected to present their closing arguments from 6am AEDT, after which the judge was expected to announce his verdict.
If convicted, the three will be sentenced on Friday.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, will address the court. Both travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 8 September.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his widow, Natalie Weirtz, will also participate in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ alleged murders as “hell.”
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.

articles.title: Afghan women facing arrest for dress code violations: UN
articles.summary: In recent months, the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan have arrested or detained dozens of women for alleged violations of dress codes and for appearing in public without a male guardian.

image.caption: In Afghanistan, women are required to wear a full hijab in public [FILE: June 2025]Image: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At least 52 women and one girl were arrested or detained in the Afghan cities of Herat and Kabul between July and September of 2026, according to a statement released by the United Nations on Thursday.

"Women were detained for not wearing a chador [an all-enveloping, cloak-like garment], having visible hair, wearing colourful scarves or makeup, or being in public without a mahram [male chaperone]," the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said.
According to the mission, the detained women were released after being held for several hours. It also warned that the number of cases could be higher due to underreporting.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban
UNAMA said it was "gravely concerned" by the arrests, detentions, and threats of arrest.

The mission stated that the detentions violate women's and girls' rights to freedom of movement, expression, and autonomy. The detentions also expose them to severe social stigma in traditional Afghan society, UNAMA said.

In June, Afghan authorities opened fire on a rare protest in Herat over the arrests and detentions of women for alleged dress code violations. According to witnesses and the UN mission, at least one person was killed and several others were injured.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan
What restrictions do women in Afghanistan face?

Since seizing power in 2021 as US-led forces withdrew from Afghanistan, the Taliban government has imposed severe restrictions on women and girls, including banning them from attending school beyond the primary level and limiting what they can wear and where they can go.

In public, women must wear a full hijab, which includes a headscarf, a long robe that covers the body, and a face covering. The Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice enforces these rules.

Earlier this week, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued four arrest warrants for senior Taliban officials, accusing them of committing crimes against humanity by systematically depriving women and girls in Afghanistan of their rights.
Hovewer, the Taliban rejected the decision, calling it a politically motivated violation of Afghanistan's sovereignty.

articles.title: Class action alleging sexual assaults at Spa Nordik to proceed
articles.summary: Dozens of people have joined a certified class action alleging they were sexually assaulted at Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., in a lawsuit that implicates dozens of massage therapists who…

image.caption: Spa Nordik Village in Chelsea, Que., just north of Ottawa. (Jean-Sébastien Marier/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa

Dozens of people have joined a certified class action alleging they were sexually assaulted at Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., in a lawsuit that implicates dozens of massage therapists who worked there over a 19-year period.
Law firm says 143 people have come forward with allegations spanning 19 years

According to the class action, filed in French in Quebec Superior Court, the popular spa just north of Ottawa and Gatineau, Que., is alleged to have improperly handled complaints and not done enough to inform and protect clients.

Lambert Avocats, the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, said 143 people contacted them in the last year saying they’d been sexually assaulted by massage therapists at Spa Nordik. The lawsuit alleges wrongdoing by a total of 36 different massage therapists at the spa between 2007 and 2026.
"People are generally pretty shocked to hear the numbers, but I think they’re also relieved to see something is being done about it and they have a recourse," said lawyer Philippe Brault.
The claims in the class action have not been tested in court.
According to the lawsuit, several of the clients who raised allegations with Spa Nordik’s management were offered gift cards "to return to the establishment where they were sexually assaulted."
'It's disturbing, it's disgusting'

The lawsuit focuses on a representative case that occurred in December 2024. CBC interviewed the woman at the centre of the complaint, who is not identified in court documents. CBC News is also not identifying her to respect the court process.
"It's disturbing, it's disgusting," she said of the number of complaints since the class action was initiated last summer.

"I represent all of the women, so that keeps me going. I want to represent them and let people know this is happening and this needs to be a situation that is managed, and these girls need to be protected and all women need to be protected and all people should be protected."

According to the court documents, the woman paid for a massage and was assigned to a male massage therapist who instructed her to undress. During the massage, he did not ease the pressure he applied despite being asked three times, according to the complaint.
It's also alleged that he touched the woman through his clothes with his stomach and genitals, and after placing a towel over her face began massaging her upper thighs.

The court documents allege Spa Nordik claimed its massage therapists were "independent contractors" and offered no apology or followup, and made no effort to prevent similar abuse following the complaint.

"This is a matter of institutional negligence," said Brault. "We want Spa Nordik and other similar establishments to understand that they have a responsibility to ensure their clients’ safety to prevent these types of events taking place, and when they know about these situations to take the proper measures to stop the situations from happening."
Client safety 'our highest priority,' spa says

The application for the class action argues Spa Nordik would have been aware of previous allegations of sexual assault before the representative case in 2024, including cases that ended up in criminal court.

The class action argues the spa should have taken steps to improve vetting and training of massage therapists, and should have better informed clients about what to expect from its services and how to report any discomfort.
Spa Nordik told CBC News in a statement that the certification of the class action is not a judgment, and it plans to defend itself.
It said the spa has taken "all necessary measures to ensure a respectful, safe and trustworthy environment."
"The safety and well-being of our guests, employees and professionals remain our highest priority," wrote Isabelle Mathieu, general manager of Nordik Spa Village.
She said the spa is unable to comment further given the ongoing legal proceedings.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matthew Kupfer has been a reporter and producer at CBC News since 2012. He can be reached at matthew.kupfer@cbc.ca and on Twitter @matthewkupfer

articles.title: Canadian investor, philanthropist Stephen Jarislowsky dies at age 101
articles.summary: Canadian investment manager, ethical business proponent and philanthropist Stephen Jarislowsky has died. He was 101.

image.caption: Stephen Jarislowsky poses in this undated handout photo. (Submitted to The Canadian Press by the Family of Stephen A. Jarislowsky)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Canadian investment manager, ethical business proponent and philanthropist Stephen Jarislowsky has died. He was 101.
He donated millions of dollars to establish dozens of research chairs at Canadian universities
Jarislowsky, who was born in Germany in 1925, founded Jarislowsky Fraser & Co. from scratch in 1955 and built the Montreal firm into what was at one point Canada's largest pension fund manager.
After working in Kingston, Ont., Montreal and New York, he returned to Montreal to found his eponymous firm with $100 of his money and $50 from a partner.
He led Jarislowsky Fraser for more than six decades before stepping down in 2012, by which time the firm was managing around $40 billion in assets.
Scotiabank bought the firm in 2018 for $950 million.

His business success made him worth some $3.9 billion US, according to Forbes, a pool of wealth he used to donate many millions of dollars including to establish dozens of research chairs at Canadian universities.

articles.title: US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
articles.summary: The Trump administration cut off tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe, from filing for green cards for their foreign workers.

image.caption: US Vice President Vance accused Microsoft of abusing a visa programImage: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.

US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.

"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.
Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.
There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.
Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards
Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.

"They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.

blocks.caption: President Trump presenting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation on October 8.Image: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans

Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.

The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.
Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report.

articles.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
articles.summary: Hundreds have pitched their tents in central Madrid, while the Spanish prime minister has called a snap election.

blocks.text: Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."
She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."
Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.

"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.
"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."
His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.

On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".
Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.

Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.
Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.
Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.
Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.

When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.

"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."
Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.
In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.
Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.

A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.
Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.

However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.
He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.
Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.
"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."
The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.
The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.

There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.
Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.
Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.
Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.
However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.

That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.
"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."

He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.
Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.

A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738).

"No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid.
"Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."
The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country.
The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

articles.title: South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent
articles.summary: A court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications reignited violent protests against immigration in South Africa.

image.caption: Protesters in Durban demanded that a refugee center stop processing asylum applicationsImage: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

blocks.text: Anti-migrant protests erupted in South Africa on Thursday as tensions over immigration were reignited by a court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications.

Some of the protests turned violent, according to local media reports. This included incidents in the coastal city of Durban and the Soweto township of Johannesburg, where cars were set on fire and gunshots were heard.
What do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban reportedly followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. About 10 vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.
Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.
At least nine vehicles were torched, said Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television.
"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," he said. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

blocks.caption: Police fired rubber bullets when clashes erupted between protesters and foreign nationals in DurbanImage: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

blocks.text: What has the court decided?
The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.
The court explained that this was because the provisions prevented individuals from accessing the asylum system on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.
Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.
On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa".
Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops
Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa
South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.
Amidst international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.
Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.
Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

articles.title: US will not resume strikes on Iran before midterms — Trump
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said the US will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterm elections on November 3. High gas and grocery prices are top concerns for voters.

image.caption: Trump said he's not going to order military strikes on Iran until after the November midterm elections [Photo: September 10]Image: Kent Nishimura/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump's announcement on social media on Thursday came after two US media outlets reported that he was weighing options to strike Iran.

The Atlantic magazine reported that the thinking was Trump would want to maintain the period of relative calm in the war with Iran until after the elections to keep the deeply unpopular war out of the news. The US has not struck the country in recent weeks.
A Pentagon official told Axios that the Department of Defense's job was to be ready for possible strikes on Iran if the president ordered them.
War abroad, soaring prices at home: is Trump in trouble?
Iran war, gas prices, and US midterms: What to know
The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire agreement in April, but that agreement didn't hold as both countries resumed fighting in the months that followed.
Trump said at the UN General Assembly that he could yet escalate the war with Iran.

But gas and fuel prices remain high in the US, with many voters already feeling the pressure of high prices for groceries and other goods — factors that have weighed on candidates in Trump's Republican Party.
Plus, the economy remains one of the top concerns for voters this midterm, when US citizens are going to be electing members of Congress.
In his social media post on Thursday, Trump also said his team has been "having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran."

That came after Trump, at the end of September, publicly rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed — to commercial shipping if the US met necessary conditions.
Then Iran last week said it had received a counterproposal.
Pentagon deploys more resources to the Middle East, WSJ reports
Trump's post also came as the military dispatched more resources to the Middle East, according to a report the Wall Street Journal.
US officials said a third aircraft-carrier strike group, and its thousands of troops, would arrive by the end of November, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
articles.summary: The German sportswear brand wants the Sydney-based label to stop selling the clothes and pay damages.

blocks.text: Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.

The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
The Australian law firms representing Adidas and White Fox both declined to comment on the case, the first hearing due to begin on Friday.
In Federal Court documents, Adidas states that its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "taking advantage" of Adidas's reputation, "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.

Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.

A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.

White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

articles.title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away
articles.summary:
Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’

A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of…

blocks.text: A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe.

Astronomers have now detected that flash, a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded.

FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin.

In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”.
The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.
The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST).
Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”.
Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”.
There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field.
“Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals”, Nanayakkara said.

More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.
Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen.
But “the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said.

This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe.
Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”.

Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.

Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].”
The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

articles.title: Alberta government to force Edmonton to change rules encouraging multiplex construction
articles.summary: The Alberta government has announced new development measures that will force Edmonton to change infill rules and alter how new homes are allowed to take shape in neighbourhoods in the province's…

image.caption: The Alberta government announced Thursday that it will direct the City of Edmonton to repeal its infill bylaws, reverting to parameters that were in place before its 2024 zoning changes. (David Bajer/CBC)

blocks.text: The Alberta government has announced it will temporarily force Edmonton to restrict the growth of infill development and review its approach to infill going forward.
The City of Edmonton overhauled its zoning bylaw to make it easier for more housing to be built, streamlining requirement and allowing multiplexes to be built on residential lots across the city.

But during a news conference Thursday, Premier Danielle Smith said the province is directing the city to repeal its zoning bylaw and revert to parameters that were in place before 2024. The province is also directing Edmonton to restore minimum on-site parking requirements that were in place before 2020.
Smith said her government is responding to residents who have complained about the character of their communities changing.
"While Edmonton has taken some steps to amend portions of its bylaws and lessen the impact in established neighborhoods, the overall approach to infill remains in place," Smith said.
"And let me be clear: the goal should not simply be more housing, but more housing that is planned and integrated in a way that works for both existing residents as well as future families."
Edmonton will have three months to amend its bylaw.

The provincial government is also requiring the City of Calgary to maintain its current pre-2024 bylaw framework, which means "returning to reasonable density and height rules, common sense minimum parking requirements and considerations for utilities and water infrastructure requirements," she said.

That city, which recently repealed blanket rezoning, will be directed to create an overlay identifying lands restored to previous low-density residential zones. This ensures requirements for housing types, building heights and parking remain in place, while its broader land-use review continues, Smith said.

As part of the interim measures announced Thursday, Alberta's two largest municipalities will also be directed to comprehensively review their land-use bylaws to develop a "more balanced" approach to infill development, Smith said.
Edmonton will have 18 months for its review, while Calgary’s broader review, which is currently underway, is planned to be completed in 2027.
Smith made Thursday's announcement in Edmonton, where the scale of recent infill development has been controversial.

items: Edmonton infill protest brings hundreds to Churchill Square

blocks.text: Supporters say the new zoning rules have led to record levels of housing being built and Edmonton maintaining its affordability. Critics have argued that large multiplexes and multi-storey buildings have strained the city's established and historic neighbourhoods.

In response to residents' frustrations, Edmonton city council has made some changes to the rules, reducing height requirements in small-scale residential zones and placing stricter setback rules for new builds.

items: Stricter infill rules coming to Edmonton, councillors say

blocks.text: Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams said Thursday that it's unusual for the province to intervene on municipal development bylaws, but necessary in this case to ensure new housing balances Albertans’ goal of home ownership in safe, affordable and livable communities.

"This announcement is about restoring the possibility for Alberta to grow in a thoughtful and balanced way. It's about giving Albertans a voice before their neighborhoods are permanently changed," he said.
The move isn't about dictating exactly what municipal residential zoning bylaws should say, he said. "Instead, it's a pause; it's a reset."

Williams credited Calgary's city council for acknowledging these concerns and repealing its 2024 rezoning changes. He said Edmonton must backtrack further on its bylaws and do more to mitigate the impacts of infill on mature neighbourhoods.
Edmonton's city administration has argued that higher-density development is needed to accommodate rapid population growth in the city and reduce the costs associated with escalating urban sprawl.
But Williams said the pace and scale of high-density development in the city has been "too far, too fast."
Rewinding creates uncertainty: expert

Edmonton's zoning bylaw reduced the number of zones in the city in order to make development more straightforward and less complex, according to Damian Collins, a housing scholar and University of Alberta professor of human geography.
Undoing that work will create a lot of uncertainty, with investment decisions — made based on the current rules — now in question, Collins told CBC News.
"Even if you don't like eight-plexes that much, the zoning bylaw deals with a lot more than just that specific housing type," he said.
Bringing back mandatory parking requirements could slow down development and create extra costs, he added.
Edmonton mayor responds

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack decried Thursday's announcement during a separate news conference. He said the province's "uninformed directive" will make the city less affordable, drive up property taxes and create months of uncertainty for Edmontonians.
"I am not entirely convinced the premier knows what she is doing, or what the consequences will be. What the premier is flirting with would cause tremendous chaos," he said.
Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack reacts to a provincial directive that the City of Edmonton repeal its zoning bylaw. (Mrinali Anchan/CBC)

The city is growing rapidly, he said, and each new suburb requires the development of expensive infrastructure — the cost of which is, ultimately, passed on to taxpayers. He said the city must focus on "smart growth" that relies on existing infrastructure, reduces sprawl and maintains affordability.
He added that now isn't the time for "partisan fights" over municipal development issues that provincial officials are not equipped to manage.

"I am focused on stable leadership and a predictable investment climate, at a time when our province is already facing so much uncertainty," he said, referring to the upcoming provincial referendum, which includes a question about Alberta's place within Canada.
Knack urged Smith to pause the initiative and work alongside city council, saying decisions about Edmonton neighbourhoods should not be made at the provincial cabinet level.
Celebration and frustration
Critics of Edmonton's zoning bylaw, who have been protesting its effects and urged the province to step in, cheered after hearing Smith announce the directive Thursday morning.

Jaclyn Soroka, a co-founder of Edmonton Neighbourhoods United, which is against the zoning changes, thanked the government for listening to residents' concerns. She said the group is not opposed to growth or change, but wants it to be responsible.
"This is about thoughtful city planning; something that affects every Edmontonian regardless of their political beliefs," Soroka said.
Jacob Dawang, an advocate with Grow Together Edmonton, which favoured the changes, said the province's announcement amounts to a war on housing affordability in Alberta's capital city.
Bylaw supporters fought hard to advocate for its passing, turning up to public hearings — as critics did — and are now feeling frustrated, he said.
A return to the old rules will lead to far fewer housing units being created, he added.

"By not building these housing options for people who can't afford a single-family home, and reducing it back to a trickle, we will be systematically excluding people from our neighbourhoods," Dawang said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 36: BIR witness reveals P85M income
articles.summary: The annual income tax returns of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, were finally opened on Day 36 of her impeachment trial--the shortest trial day so far.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 1:45am
The annual income tax returns of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, were finally opened on Day 36 of her impeachment trial—the shortest trial day so far.

Private prosecutor Erwin Matib, who was scheduled to conduct direct examination of the prosecution's witness from the Breau of Internal Revenue (BIR), Atty. Anne Marquez, called in sick at the 11th hour.
The prosecution tried to remedy the situation by offering to present another witness, financial analyst and tax expert Alex Cabrera.
This was, however, opposed by the defense lead counsel, Sheila Sison, arguing that last-minute switching of witnesses won’t be fair to the respondent Vice President.
This prompted the Senate impeachment court to suspend the trial from 10:42 pm until 2:30 pm.
When it resumed, Matib showed up and conducted his cross-examination of Marquez, paving the way for the revelation of the Vice President and her husband's tax returns for the very first time.
Marquez then testified that the Vice President and her husband recorded P85.3 million worth of income from 2007 to 2025.

In addition, the BIR official told the Senate impeachment court that Vice President Sara Duterte reported P1.058 million in “other income” on top of her compensation income in 2024, and another P1.082 million in 2025.

The BIR official also said that the Vice President received compensation income from Davao City government in 2023, and that the BIR already issued a Letter of Authority to the Vice President and her husband.

The BIR defines the Letter of Authority (LOA) as “BIR's primary legal document that authorizes revenue officers to examine a taxpayer's books and records” and “a document that grants the Commissioner the authority to conduct audits based on a clear legal foundation, with proper identification of the examiner and adherence to due process.”
In a later press conference, private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. said such P85 million in income cannot account for the couple's P98 million declared net worth as of 2025.
Mans’ links to Cale88 still exist

Marquez also told the Senate impeachment court that based on BIR database, there are no records arising from or in connection with any transfer, sale, disposition, or other conveyance of shares of stock of Kale 88 Foods Corporation owned by Atty. Carpio, the husband of the Vice President.

“In relation thereto, no documents or records were found evidencing the payment, assessment, or settlement of any applicable taxes, fees, or other charges arising from or in connection with such transfer or disposition,” Marquez said.
Cale88 Foods Corporation is a declared asset of the Vice President’s husband in multiple years, but was removed as one in their joint SALN filing in 2025.

Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer was able to start her cross-examination on Thursday, but she asked that she be allowed to stop at 6 pm and continue it tomorrow since she will take approximately two more hours.
The trial ended at 6:07 pm.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem
articles.summary:
Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city

Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in…

blocks.text: Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said.

The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control.
Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite to the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London.

That is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world.

Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding with plans to bar trade with West Bank settlements and put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing.

The UK threatened to respond with a mass expulsion of diplomats but the two countries appear to have backed away from a full-blown diplomatic spat as Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October.

Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume.

Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who has advised western diplomats including a British foreign secretary.
“The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said.
“The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.”

blocks.caption: Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, one expert said.  Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: There are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries.

They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine.

Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions.

“This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.”
Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies.
The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency.

The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretz reported on Thursday.

An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for the E1 settlement in the West Bank.

When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank.

Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”.
The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate was a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said.
Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said.

articles.title: France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally
articles.summary: Police fired tear gas and used batons against protesters in Paris again as students continue to voice their grievances about school conditions across France.

image.caption: Student demonstrators complained about absent teachers, long schedules and dilapidated classrooms unable to cope with rising temperaturesImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: Thousands of students demonstrated near Bastille Square in Paris on Thursday afternoon, as France's nationwide student protests continue.
Crowds of students climbed the famous Bastille Monument. Some waved the French flag and sang the national anthem.
Footage from Reuters TV showed riot police charging at protesters with batons as they moved in to clear the square.

blocks.caption: Protesters marched toward the Place de la Bastille during a demonstration in ParisImage: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP

blocks.text: Students barricade high school
Earlier on Thursday, students barricaded Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris with trash bins before police broke up the protest with tear gas.
As students gathered at the school, riot police assembled in the side streets. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid identification.
The school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday.
Although the rallies have largely been peaceful, some demonstrators have set fires and vandalized bus shelters.

blocks.caption: Since the beginning of the protests in September, the French police have made more than 6,600 arrestsImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: In response, the police have used tear gas, batons, and blast balls. Human rights groups and children accuse officers of using excessive force.
Following an incident in which a teenager's hand was blown off, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control on Wednesday.
Since late September, when students, most of whom are under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, police have made more than 6,600 arrests, according to the Interior Ministry.
France students demand better schools
Government promises response
On Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised that the government would present "concrete, quick, and fully funded responses" to the protests by the end of October.
Nevertheless, student protest leaders said this was not good enough and called for more marches.

In a televised address, Lecornu also lamented the "violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults."

articles.title: What we know about Ottawa's $2B rebate plan for heat pumps

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Dettson, a manufacturer of residential and commercial HVAC systems in Sherbrooke, Que., on Thursday, where he announced a new $2-billion rebate program. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Canada's federal government has announced a new $2-billion rebate plan aimed at getting more heat pumps installed in homes across the country in the years ahead.
Program to formally launch early 2027, but may be made retroactive to fall
Initial details of the National Heat Pump Rebate Program were announced Thursday.
Here's what we know so far.
How many households will benefit?
The Government of Canada says up to 820,000 households will be able to take advantage of the rebate program, over an eight-year period.
How soon does it start?
The government expects to launch the rebate early next year. But Ottawa is eyeing making it retroactive to fall.
How does it work?
Homeowners will be able to apply for the rebate when their existing heating system breaks down — or when they plan to replace a heating system that is approaching end of life.

Government data suggests 80 per cent of HVAC replacements occur when current systems break. The new program is trying to cater to this group of individuals — and provide a path to switching over to heat pumps accordingly.
Ottawa launching $2B rebate program for home heat pumps
Applications for the rebate will be filed via an online portal. The government says approvals will be confirmed within 24 hours.

Homeowners will submit receipts after installation of the pre-approved heat pumps, so that rebates can follow — with payment to be "approved within five days," according to a government document outlining aspects of the new program.
The payments that follow will be made via direct deposit.
How much is the rebate worth?
Up to $10,000 for households below the median income. Other eligible households can claim $2,000.
What kind of heat pumps will be eligible?

Homeowners will be able to look to a list of eligible products, which the government says will include "an extensive selection of over 100,000 options at various price points and configurations, all suited for the Canadian climate."
Will energy audits be required?
No.
What happens next?
The government says it will be consulting with industry and work with HVAC installers to maximize the reach of the pending program.
Government officials who briefed media said that Ottawa wants industry to have the needed inventory on hand to deliver the program as planned. This is one reason why consultations are taking place.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: ICC Registry advises judges: Duterte's unexplained exits could fuel disinformation
articles.summary: As the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte nears, the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry is asking Trial Chamber III to consider explaining its authorizations before allowing him to…
articles.byline: Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan, Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 12:53am

As the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte nears, the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry is asking Trial Chamber III to consider explaining its authorizations before allowing him to leave the courtroom.
In its observations published on October 7, the Registry said victims and affected communities have shown “strong interest” in following Duterte’s trial live, particularly from the Philippines.

For people watching the trial online, the Registry said the concern could be even greater if Duterte suddenly disappears from the courtroom feed without explanation as it could fuel speculation and disinformation.

“This would create fertile ground for disinformation and speculations [sic], e.g., about his health, which is a recurring topic of interest in the Philippines, or the effect that his leaving and entering the courtroom could have on a witness.”
To avoid this, the Registry proposed that any standing permission for Duterte to leave the courtroom be publicly explained on the first day of trial.
It said judges should give “as much concrete details as possible” about the arrangement and could repeat a brief explanation at the start of each trial day.
The Registry also said witnesses should be informed in advance if such an arrangement is in place.
“Very intensive” coverage
The Registry also expects that Philippine media would follow the proceedings “very intensively”, including “smallest details”.
“Journalists are certain to pay attention to the smallest details related to Mr Duterte’s appearance and conduct,” it said.
The Registry also said victims and affected communities place “paramount importance” on Duterte’s presence during the proceedings.

If Duterte does not attend in person, another option is a video link from the ICC Detention Center, subject to the Chamber’s approval. The Registry said he would still be able to communicate privately with his lawyers under that setup.
In a decision, Trial Chamber III has found Duterte fit for trial, stating he “he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.”
It has also instructed the ICC Registry to “make necessary arrangements”, including a sitting schedule.
The fourth status conference is scheduled for October 13. The final one before the trial proceedings is set for November 2. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary
articles.summary:
Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians

The Israeli government is promoting an online film…

blocks.text: The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings.
The real documentary, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries.
The Israeli government has denounced the film and announced plans to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason.

In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians, toward claims that it is the “most moral army in the world”.
Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party.

The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history.

Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened.

“Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’s official synopsis by removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians.
That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.

It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.)

According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team.
The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commission has described as genocide.

The 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”.

The Israeli government said on Thursday that it was awarding the filmmakers with a certificate of appreciation “for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views.

A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary.
“This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.”
As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

Averbuch is the founder of an organisation which says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025.
Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.

The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship.

Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.

On Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram.

Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”
Additional reporting by Philip McMahon

articles.title: Zambia signs US health deal after disputes over data-sharing
articles.summary: The US will provide $1.5bn (£1.1bn) under the deal that was negotiated after Trump cut USAID funding.

blocks.text: Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid.
Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing.

Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied.
The deal comes after the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was cut.

US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost.
Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens.
Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing.

Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records.
Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal.

A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens.

The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published.
Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals.

In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false.
The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed.

Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers.

The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending.
Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied.

Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding.

Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach.
The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic.
Additional reporting by Mallory Moench

articles.title: US prosecutors add new torture charge against Maduro
articles.summary: US prosecutors have added a new charge to their case against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing the couple of conspiring to commit torture.

image.caption: Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the US [FILE: January 5, 2026]Image: Adam Gray/REUTERS

blocks.text: US prosecutors have announced new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents and US citizens
The new charges against the couple are in addition to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced, according to a revised indictment released Thursday.
Both Maduro and Flores have denied the previous charges brought against them.
Revised indictment adds pressure on Maduro
The revised indictment alleged that the couple committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.
High tensions between the US and a socialist and oil-rich Venezuela were a constant during Maduro's 13 years in power.
Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

"He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," the indictment said.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.
Maduro's wife seeks release from New York jail
Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday. She is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11.4 kilograms) in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

blocks.caption: Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing US nationals [FILE: March 26, 2026]Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.
They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary while in custody.
Trump vs. Maduro
Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.
The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."
Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.
They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.
Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."
Venezuelans want elections — but when will they get them?

articles.title: EU pulls sponsorship from Disinfo2026 event in Lithuania
articles.summary: The EU's diplomatic service, Canada and host nation Lithuania all pulled support from a disinformation event in Vilnius. Amid reports of US pressure, the EU said it was "uncomfortable with the…

image.caption: The conference took place at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius, but without several of its pre-planned backers [FILE: August 12, 2025]Image: Joko/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union on Thursday offered its reasons for withdrawing sponsorship for a disinformation event in Lithuania, following media reports claiming that it did so after pressure from the US government.

The EU's foreign affairs division, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the governments of Canada and Lithuania all pulled their support from the event at short notice. Sponsors' logos on flyers and placards at the event were hastily covered over with paper strips.
They withdrew participation in Disinfo2026 after pressure from the US State Department, according to reports in several media outlets, including the British newspaper The Guardian.
What did the EU say about its decision?
EU spokesperson Christian Wigand made no mention of the US or external pressure on Thursday but also did not repudiate the reports.
"We were not comfortable with the framing of some of the discussions at the event," he told reporters in Brussels.
"The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU," he said.
He refused to discuss details of which discussions or what framing had perturbed the EEAS. He also would not comment on whether there had been talks with US officials on the matter.
"I'm not commenting on diplomatic exchanges as a matter of principle," he said.
What signs of potential controversy at Disinfo2026 were visible?

While a number of the sessions planned on the event's website across two days at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius appeared to have the potential to perturb more sensitive members of Donald Trump's administration, the opening two sessions on Wednesday morning stood out.

The opening of the conference was an interview with Kimberly Prost, a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has come under sustained and heavy fire from Trump and his administration during his second term.

This was followed by an hourlong session entitled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back," using the acronym for Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference. One of the planned speakers was a former CIA officer.

Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth.

articles.title: Sask., Alberta premiers reject Elon Musk's call for provinces to separate from Canada
articles.summary: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk: "No." Alberta's Danielle Smith also disagrees with Musk's suggestion.

image.caption: Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No." (Alexander Quon/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk: "No." Alberta's Danielle Smith also disagrees with Musk's suggestion.
Elon Musk suggested Alberta and Saskatchewan would be better off separating from Canada
The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan have rejected a suggestion by one of the world's richest men that the two provinces should separate from Canada.
Musk, a trillionaire tech businessman who was formerly an advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, weighed in on his social media platform Twitter, now known as X.
Musk said Quebec would benefit from independence, as would Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The tech tycoon was responding to a quote from Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who said the province's independence "will be realized one day."
Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No."
Moe was not available for an interview on Thursday and his office said he had nothing more to add to the post.
According to the Canadian Press, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she also strongly disagrees with Musk's opinion.

items: Alberta separatists see ally in Quebec premier-designate St-Pierre Plamondon

blocks.text: The state of play in each province
On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.
Smith has said she plans to vote to stay in Canada in the upcoming provincial referendum.
Moe believes Saskatchewan is stronger within a united Canada, but has previously said he would not stop a plebiscite if Saskatchewanians were able to secure enough signatures to trigger a referendum.
Moe has also enjoyed a much better relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney than with his predecessor Justin Trudeau.
Why Saskatchewan's premier says Trump's potash threats are 'not realistic'
Moe has at various times refused to say Trudeau's name even after his departure from federal politiccs.
In Quebec, the sovereigntist Parti Québécois is back in power after a securing enough seats to form a minority government in Monday's provincial election.
Soon-to-be premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold a referendum.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexander Quon is the provincial affairs reporter for CBC Saskatchewan. He has been a reporter with CBC Saskatchewan since 2021 and is happy to be working in his hometown of Regina after half a decade in Atlantic Canada. He has previously worked with the CBC News investigative unit in Nova Scotia and Global News in Halifax. Alexander specializes in freedom of information requests and data reporting. He can be reached at: alexander.quon@cbc.ca.
