articles.title: Researchers find 180,000 giant tortoises living on island in Seychelles
articles.summary:
Figure is highest ever recorded for species and confirms one of Indian Ocean’s greatest conservation success stories

A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise…

blocks.text: A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoise lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island.
This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.
It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve.
“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

blocks.caption: There are more giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll than humans. Photograph: Avalon.red/Alamy

blocks.text: The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island.
But a recovery programme meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.

“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
after newsletter promotion

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors warn that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

articles.title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
articles.summary:
Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack…

blocks.text: Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into the Tigray region on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and conflict monitoring group Acled.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.

Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.

In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups within Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.

blocks.caption: Members of the Ethiopian republican guards patrol at the Mekelle Alula Aba Nega international airport on Wednesday. Photograph: Obtained by Reuters

blocks.text: Eritrea’s information minister Yemane Gebremeskel said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”

The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of committing war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister Abiy Ahmed a Nobel Peace prize.

blocks.caption: Pro-government forces in Mekelle, Ethiopia, on Wednesday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, with state media claiming that it has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US war with Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.

In its Monday statement, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”

Gebremeskel, Eritrea’s information minister, said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to re-package this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”

Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at Crisis Group, a thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try and solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”
While the full impact of the ongoing fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight.

“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”
Associated Press contributed to this story

articles.title: How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting countries on Africa's Red Sea coast — and beyond
articles.summary: Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemeni government forces are trying to take back from the Houthis, is located not far from Djibouti and other African states.

image.caption: A Yemeni soldier pictured patrolling the Red Sea in AprilImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In September, one of the major conflicts in the Middle East came within sight of Africa, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Yemen's Perim Island.

The island forms the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the southern entrance of the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Djibouti and 20-minutes by air to Ethiopia.
In early October, Yemen's armed forces and their Saudi allies launched a counteroffensive. TheIran-backed Houthis have been firing on merchant ships since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.
The economic consequences for Africa is coupled with a refugee inflow
African economies are already suffering from crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, which is making particularly fuel and fertilizer scarce and more expensive.

If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also becomes impassable, the situation could deteriorate further. Shipping companies would have to make detours via the Suez Canal, which is controlled by Egypt or the southern tip of Africa, as some already do. The additional costs would be passed on to consumers.

The human cost of the escalation in Yemen hit Djibouti almost immediately. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), at least 3,700 refugees have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10. Most of those who made it to the country's northern Obock region are women and children.
The UNHCR is preparing to assist another 10,000 people who have not yet crossed into Djibouti. But Obock, which is on the border with Eritrea, is extremely dry and this is causing other issues.
"We don't have much water here; there's no groundwater at all," Alessandra Roccasalvo, the UN Development Program (UNDP) representative for Djibouti, told DW. "Everything has to be desalinated."
Thousands flee to Djibouti from Yemen's war
Djibouti is a strategic military hub

Despite its small size, Djibouti — a Muslim-majority Horn of Africa country with a population of just over a million — is a major player in the region. Its position at at the entrance to the Red Sea makes it an attractive commercial and military shipping hub.
The United States, China, France, Italy, and Japan all operate military bases in Djibouti. The German Bundeswehr was also present until 2021, as part of a naval mission to combat maritime piracy.
The country's civilian ports serve as transshipment, or intermediate, hubs for global shipping cargo, goods and containers. So far, the Houthi advance has not led to empty docks in Djibouti.

But there are still potential consequences, said Roccasalvo: "Basically, there's an economic upswing here — which means, as in any country experiencing an upswing, building materials are needed: cement, raw materials, and other things."

Less of that money is now coming in because ships have to pay nearly twice as much for insurance and reinsurance as they used to. "Many ships no longer want to pass through the Suez Canal; many no longer want to pass through the Red Sea."
Knock-on effects for landlocked neighboring Ethiopia

Ethiopia — the world's most populous landlocked country — handles about 95% of its imports and exports through Djibouti's ports. Price hikes resulting from higher war-risk shipping insurance premiums are affecting the country greatly.
Shortly after the Houthis seized Perim, Ethiopia's economy faced another, even more immediate threat: On September 23, fighting broke out in the country's northern Tigray region.

Since then, the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) have reportedly made gains against the Tigray-led rebel coalition that aims to overthrow the national government. The rebels briefly advanced toward the main corridor used for transporting goods between Djibouti's ports and the Ethiopian hinterland.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again

According to certain experts, the ENDF's advances have since reduced the threat of yet another trade blockade — but as long as the conflict remains unresolved, the situation could potentially deteriorate again.

For months now, Ethiopia has suffered more than almost any other African country from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has already had to ration fuel at times. In the long term, the country aims to reduce its dependence on imports, for example by powering vehicles with domestically generated electricity instead of imported gasoline.

blocks.caption: In early 2024, Ethiopia became the first country in the world to impose a ban on the import of internal combustion engine vehiclesImage: Shewangizaw Wegayehu/DW

blocks.text: Can the conflict in Ethiopia affect Bab el-Mandeb access?
Ethiopia and its northern neighbor, Eritrea, have severed diplomatic ties; other regional powers such as Sudan, Egypt, and Somalia may find themselves siding with Eritrea rather than with Ethiopia.

Eritrea sees itself as facing a threat that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has reiterated on several occasions: With Ethiopia deprived of access to the sea since Eritrea's independence, Abiy has often alluded to rectifying this perceived injustice — either through a political agreement, as was once sought with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland, or by force.

The port of Assab is located on the edge of Eritrea's panhandle — and is often described as the most likely target should Abiy choose the path of aggression. If the fighting within Ethiopia further escalates into a full-blown regional war, this could also lead to additional restrictions on safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the surrounding waters.

Experts have also raised concerns about the Shiite Houthis increasingly collaborating with the Sunni terrorist group Al-Shabab, which is based in Somalia. Although their ideologies are fundamentally different, they are united by their hostility toward Israel and the US among other things.
Inside Somalia's arms smuggling network
What tools are at the disposal of African countries to help remedy the situation?

The three African non-permanent members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia — held an emergency meeting in mid-September on this issue, during which they jointly called for free shipping lanes and endorsed the demand that the crisis in Yemen be resolved under the auspices of the UN.

blocks.caption: Liberia's UN Ambassador Lews Garseedah Brown has formulated joint principles with his counterparts from Somalia and the Congo: the African nations are hoping for a UN-led diplomatic solution for YemenImage: Bianca Otero/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The situation at Bab el-Mandeb and in northern Ethiopia is once again demanding flexibility from Africa. In fact, some African economies can also benefit from relocation activities: Ports inKenya and Tanzania, for example, are becoming increasingly attractive for transshipment.
And while many countries are suffering from high oil prices, Nigeria's Dangote Group has announced an initial public offering and a new refinery in Kenya.
This article was originally published in German. It has been updated.

articles.title: Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
articles.summary:
Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousands

The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to…

blocks.text: The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners.

Parviz Sabeti, who was reported last year to have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government was posted on social media by his daughter.

He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in the detention and torture of thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979.
Sabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or that Savak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “always opposed torture”.

Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor.

In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended.

Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida.

In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim.

They included the Guardian’s September 2025 story that chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”.

As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secret analysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018.

According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the most powerful and feared men in the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”.

The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah by Savak, Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction.

Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time.

The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears.

Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A 2023 report on the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work.
Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication.
after newsletter promotion

Claret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims.

“I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said.
“Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades.

“We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].”

Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US.
Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, has positioned himself as a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support.
In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced to distance himself from far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies.

Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activist Masood Masjoody, a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader.
According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.

articles.title: DOJ: Leviste not yet a fugitive from justice
articles.summary: Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste has not been tagged as a fugitive from justice, Department of Justice (DOJ) acting Senior Deputy State Prosecutor Herbert Calvin Abugan clarified yesterday.

blocks.text: October 9, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste has not been tagged as a fugitive from justice, Department of Justice (DOJ) acting Senior Deputy State Prosecutor Herbert Calvin Abugan clarified yesterday.
“As of now, not yet. There’s a process that needs to be followed before we can declare him fugitive from justice,” Abugan explained, referring to the court’s processes.

Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida earlier noted the prosecutors handling Leviste’s case may make use of tools such as tagging him a fugitive from justice, canceling his passport and requesting an Interpol red notice, only when the embattled lawmaker submits to law enforcement through arrest or surrender.

“The prosecutors will control where the journey of the case will go. There is a process there, fugitive from justice, cancellation of passport, those are tools that can be used by prosecutors for any accused to recognize the jurisdiction of the court,” he said.
No big deal?
Vida disputed Leviste’s claim that the case against him before a court in Makati City was a “small matter.”
Leviste’s case for the failure of his firm Solar Para sa Bayan Corp. to comply with obligations under its congressional franchise should be a “big deal” for him, Vida declared.
“It’s a big deal. Why? Not obeying or following the law is big deal. Our respect for the court and its processes like arrest warrants is a big thing,” Vida said in a media briefing at DOJ yesterday.
He also took a swipe at Leviste and his mother Sen. Loren Legarda, who both reportedly flew to France over her supposed medical issues in August this year.
“We know that Congressman Leviste is a lawmaker, as well as his mother… We are just following the law that they passed because it aims to bring order,” Vida added.
He slammed Leviste’s remark that the case – with bail set at P72,000 – was “just a small matter compared to everything else that’s happening.”
“The P72,000 may be a small thing for him, but it’s not about the amount. What is important here is respect for the law,” Vida said.
The DOJ has urged Leviste to “submit himself to the jurisdiction of the court before he may avail himself of his bail, either through arrest or voluntary surrender.”

articles.title: Stronger protection vs inflation sought
articles.summary: Sen. Bong Go has called for stronger measures to protect Filipinos from rising living costs after the country’s headline inflation accelerated to 7.2 percent in September.

blocks.text: October 9, 2026 | 12:00am
One of the primary drivers of the increase was food and non-alcoholic beverages, wherein inflation accelerated to 6.7 percent from 4.6 percent the previous month, the PSA said.
STAR / Andy Zapata Jr.
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Bong Go has called for stronger measures to protect Filipinos from rising living costs after the country’s headline inflation accelerated to 7.2 percent in September.

Concerned state agencies should intensify price monitoring, address supply bottlenecks affecting essential commodities and ensure that government assistance programs remain responsive to families hit by rising prices, Go said.
Data released by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) on Oct. 6 showed that headline inflation rose to 7.2 percent in September from 6.1 percent in August.
The latest figure brought average inflation from January to September to 5.4 percent.
Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels registered an inflation of 8.4 percent, while transportation recorded 14.6 percent.
Health-related prices rose by 5.6 percent.

Government interventions should prioritize sectors with the least financial flexibility, including poor families, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, workers earning modest incomes, farmers, fisherfolk and other vulnerable groups, Go said.

articles.title: DepEd to evaluate aging classrooms
articles.summary: Classrooms existing for 50 years will be assessed by the Department of Education.

blocks.text: October 9, 2026 | 12:00am

“Demolishing these classrooms would not be automatic once they turn 50 years old. We would assess the actual condition of these classrooms. If these old classrooms are still stable, we would extend their useful life,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said yesterday.
AFP / Arnold Almacen
MANILA, Philippines — Classrooms existing for 50 years will be assessed by the Department of Education (DepEd).

“If there are repairs that need to be made, whether big or small, we would immediately conduct the repairs. The demolition and changing (of the classrooms) are only reserved for those structures that are really no longer safe and no longer practical to fix,” he added.
Citing data from the Second Congressional Commission on Education, the DepEd said there would be 51,222 classrooms existing for 50 years by 2028.
Under the DepEd’s evaluation framework, classrooms in good condition continue to be used and maintained, extending their operational lifespan by about 15 years.
In the agency’s budget, funds allocated for maintenance and other operating expenses are used to add 10 years of serviceability to facilities requiring basic maintenance and repair.
Structures requiring significant work undergo repairs that are technically feasible and safe, extending operational life by five years.
Facilities considered structurally compromised or beyond repair are scheduled for demolition and replacement.
Based on its long-term planning, the DepEd projects 18,132 classrooms per year may require replacement between 2026 and 2030 and 18,380 classrooms per year between 2031 and 2035.
Education budget inadequate – Diokno
Key DepEd programs that need substantial funding have been stripped of allocation in the 2027 national budget, prompting a lawmaker to denounce the “inadequate funding.”

Rep. Chel Diokno cited, among others, the Last Mile Schools program, an initiative that provides resources and facilities in schools in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, which “received zero allocation again.”

Other programs include the proposed increase for the school-based feeding program, learner support programs and support to operations – all of which requested additional allocation, but were “not granted” funding.
“I urge my fellow lawmakers to allocate sufficient resources where the need is greatest and where they can have the greatest impact on the lives of the Filipino learners,” Diokno said.
While some programs received additional funding, the amounts remained significantly below their proposed increases, he noted.
Diokno said the education budget did not grow at all in the House version, which was unacceptable, especially with the learning crisis that the country continues to face. – Delon Porcalla

articles.title: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering, rights group says
articles.summary: More than 500 migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, HRW says, citing US data.

blocks.text: Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration.
"Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets".
Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election.
Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently.
According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture".
The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention.

In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said.

The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere".
"The point is to scare people," HRW said.

"Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director.

In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them."
None of the African countries named has commented on the report.

However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected".
HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.

Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water".
"The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says.
According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations.
Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity.
In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo.
He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture.

In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries.
"The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said.
Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said.
Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte ruled fit to stand trial by ICC judges
articles.summary: Judges at the International Criminal Court said Rodrigo Duterte was fit to understand the charges at his trial, which is set to begin in November. His legal team argued that he suffers from cognitive…

image.caption: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte was ruled fit for trial Image: Piroschka van de Wouw/AFP

blocks.text: Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) said Thursday that former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is competent to stand trial on charges of crimes against humanity.
Duterte walked into the courtroom for his first-ever in-person appearance at a hearing last month after a year of having been detained at The Hague, where the global court is located.
Judges at the court this April confirmed charges against him, accusing him of murder and attempted murder for his alleged role in the killings of dozens of people during his "war on drugs."
Duterte's trial is set to begin on November 30. He faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.
Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte
Duterte makes his first appearance in court after being arrested
Duterte did not speak at a hearing last month but sipped water throughout the proceedings.
His legal team has argued that he suffers from cognitive decline that affects his memory and daily functioning.
ICC judges in January said his health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court. He had missed several hearings or attended those via videolink.
Now, the ICC's ruling, dated September 28 and made public on Thursday, clears the road for his trial to get underway.

The court ruling said an independent panel of experts found Duterte "has the capacity to understand the charges" and follow the proceedings, including the implication of entering a plea — which he will be asked to do when the trial opens.
He also is mentally fit to understand evidence and discuss his defense with his lawyers, the panel of experts said.
Duterte's violent anti-narcotics campaign

Duterte was arrested last year on accusations of crimes that took place during his "war on drugs" campaign when he was president between 2016 and 2022 and before that, when he was mayor of Davao City.
The charges against him are tied to brutal killings that took place on his watch between November 2011 and March 2019.

Duterte's campaign to wipe out the use of illegal narcotics in the country ended with the deaths of thousands of people as police systematically targeted poor and defenseless people, according to Amnesty International.
Prosecutors alleged that police and hit squad members carried out dozens of murders at Duterte's behest starting in 2011, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.
Philippines: Duterte 'must face reckoning' for drug war

articles.title: Sara Duterte, husband's P85 million income from 2007-2025 doesn't match net worth
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carprio, recorded P85.3 million income from 2007 to 2025, a witness from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) told the impeachment court Thursday.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 11:30pm
Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carprio, recorded P85.3 million income from 2007 to 2025, a witness from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) told the impeachment court Thursday.
Lawyer Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, chief of staff of BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza, made the testimony during Day 36 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President.
“The income net of tax from 2007 to 2025 for spouses Manasas Carpio and Sara Duterte, based on our summary, is ₱85,343,803.23,” Garcia-Marquez said.
“Income net of tax pertains to all income, less than deductions or expenses, and taxes due to a taxpayer,” Garcia-Marquez added.

The BIR official also testified that the Vice President recorded P1.058 million worth of what she identified as other income on top of her compensation income in 2024, and that the Vice President posted another P1.082 million in other income outside of her compensation income in 2025.
“[These are] Audited Financial Statements that the taxpayer [Vice President] submitted as an attachment to her income tax return,” she added.

In a separate press conference, private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. said the P85 million of the Duterte-Carpio couple from 2007 to 2025 raises questions given that their latest net worth declaration in their joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth as of 2025 is already at P98 million.

“Their net worth increased by P91 million from 2007 to 2025. Now, compare this with the declared income net of taxes, which is P85.34 million. Ang question roon, paano nangyari na iyong itinaas ng net worth mo e mas malaki sa dineklara mo during the same period?” Tolosa said.
(How come that the amount of your net worth increase exceeded your declared income?)

“And you have to take to consideration, you still have living expenses. But kahit nga sabihin mo na in 19 years, wala kang ginastos, lahat ng kinita mo tinago mo, kaya dumagdag lahat yan sa net worth mo. Kailangan pa rin sagutin ‘yung katanungan: bakit sumobra pa rin [ang net worth sa kita mo ayon sa BIR]? Tolosa added.

(Even if you did not touch your income for 19 years and you kept them all, and this accounted for your increase in net worth. The question remains: Why is your net worth bigger than your declared income?)

The prosecution is presenting evidence to prove Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President: amassed unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Thousands to march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
articles.summary:
Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis

Thousands of people are expected to march through the centre of Madrid…
articles.byline: Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid

blocks.text: Thousands of people are expected to march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis.
The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night.

Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election, to be held on 29 November.

Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”.

Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.”

For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.”

Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.”

Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.”

He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.”
The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat.

“Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media. “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.”

Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office.
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
after newsletter promotion
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.”

The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office.

PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties.

Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa, while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint.

At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved. Another wrote: “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”

Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas.
Human rights groups in Venezuela and former prisoners have long denounced what they have described as "systematic torture" in Venezuelan jails.

The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.

articles.title: French students vow to continue protests, saying ministers’ pledges not enough
articles.summary: Schools blockaded again across country as teenagers and teachers demand more investment and ‘concrete measures’ to improve conditions

blocks.text: High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign despite government pledges to address the grievances underlying 10 days of protests that have left hundreds injured.

Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a procession marched through the city centre to arrive at the Place de la Bastille.

Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.

blocks.caption: Crowds gathered at the Place de la Bastille on Thursday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

blocks.text: The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said after meeting students and teachers on Thursday at a school in the eastern city of Reims that he was “implementing an emergency plan to ensure absent teachers can be replaced on a long-term basis”.

Heavy timetables were also under review, Geffray said, as were changes to the widely criticised university application system. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised a “concrete, rapid and fully funded” response by the end of the month.

Students said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, president of one high school student’s union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.

Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table” – the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.

According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.

blocks.caption: Burning bins during a blockade of a school in Toulouse on Thursday. Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the county’s high schools were at least partly open.

But several marches drew up to 5,000 protesters, and the demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.

A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Protesters clashing with French gendarmes in Nantes on Thursday. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters

blocks.text: Over the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.

At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers had been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days.

The government on Wednesday suspended the use of stun grenades by police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.

The protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.

The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.

Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.
Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

articles.title: 2026 Nobel Prize winner Anne Carson: Where to start reading
articles.summary: The works of this year's Nobel Literature Prize-winning poet and essayist Anne Carson can feel slightly daunting. Here are some keys to understanding her universe.

image.caption: Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize for Literature on October 8, 2026Image: Hannah McKay/REUTERS

blocks.text: "You remember too much,
my mother said to me recently.
Why hold onto all that? And I said,
Where can I put it down?"

This quote is from the long, lyrical poem "The Glass Essay" published in Anne Carson's 1995 collection "Glass, Irony and God" — an entry point into the works of the 2026 Nobel Prize for Literature laureate.

In the poem, the narrator explores the burden of memory and obsessive desire after a failed love affair, all while regularly reflecting on Emily Brontë — an author renowned for her intense literary depiction of destructive and passionate love in "Wuthering Heights."

The poem brings several of Carson's recurring obsessions together into one work. She has repeatedly written about desire, abandonment and jealousy, and has often used other literary figures as emotional doubles, as historical anchor points to her ideas.

In a way, "The Glass Essay" encapsulates Carson's method; the Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist has often intellectualized emotional themes by intertwining her personal reflections with analysis, etymology, translation, literary history and philosophical thought.
Another trademark of her work is the genre fludity found in "The Glass Essay," which — as the title indicates — is partly a literary criticism essay, even though it is also a poem due to its form.

"Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," noted Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel Committee, in his description of the Nobel laureate on October 8.

blocks.caption: Carson, who now lives in Iceland, told the Nobel Prize committee she was 'listening to the wind' when they reached her with the news of the awardImage: Pontus Lundahl/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: Finding Greek mythology in a shopping mall

Born in the Canadian city of Toronto, Carson first developed her fascination for ancient Greek myths as a teenager. She told literary journal The Brick that she spotted a bilingual edition of "Sappho" by Willis Barnstone in the display of a bookstore of a shopping mall in Ontario, and that had led her to ask a high school Latin teacher to teach her ancient Greek.
She went on to publish her doctoral thesis in Classics, entitled "Odi et Amo Ergo Sum" (I hate and I love, therefore I am).

Carson's first book of criticism, "Eros the Bittersweet," was published in 1986. It lays the foundation of her approach, as she draws on ancient Greek writers such as Sappho and Plato to examine how desire — and the obstacles between the lover and the beloved — creates emotional tension.
The book suggests that the ache of wanting is not separate from love; it is one of the things that makes desire so powerful.
A Greek myth turned into a queer coming-of-age story

Because "Eros the Bittersweet" moves between Greek poetry, philosophy and literary criticism and personal interpretations, it is not considered a conventionally easy read. A more immediately engaging work and good starting point to discover Carson is the verse novel "Autobiography of Red," published in 1998.
"Autobiography of Red" was inspired by the ancient Greek myth of Heracles (or Hercules) and the red-winged monster Geryon, which the hero kills as his 10th task in his series of 12 monumental labors.

An otherwise minor figure from mythology, Geryon is turned into Heracles' lover in Carson's book. She reimagines the myth as a modern, queer coming-of-age story, with the monster experiencing love, jealousy, sexuality and heartbreak.
"We all feel we're monsters most of the time," explained Carson.
The work is accessible, funny and moving, and no deep knowledge of Greek mythology is required to enjoy it.

blocks.caption: Anne Carson makes ancient Greek myths feel modern and turns human experiences of love, grief and loneliness into poetry that's moving and unexpectedImage: Hannah McKay/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pop culture meets classics

The key to reading Carson is not to expect every connection to be immediately clear. Her books reward curiosity rather than certainty, and her sprawling, non-linear web of knowledge can be compared to going down a hyperlinked rabbit hole of narrative ideas.

"Men in the Off Hours" (2000) is another intellectually playful collection of poems. Here Carson collides the modern with the ancient, with references to figures as diverse as Beethoven, Virginia Woolf, Emily Dickinson, Jean-Luc Godard, Sigmund Freud, Homer and Hokusai.
The poems bring together fragments of history, mythology and ordinary life, allowing unexpected emotional and intellectual connections to emerge.

In the spoken and sung performance piece "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), Carson similarly brings together classical and pop culture, reimagining the story of Helen of Troy alongside the life and cultural image of Marilyn Monroe.
A tango with a deceiving beauty
How do people become the victims of desires they cannot control? This is a core theme Carson explores in "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos," published in 2001.

It features the Canadian author's wry humor in a powerful and moving way, with erotic, painful and heartbreaking scenes from a doomed marriage: a 30-year obsession with a pathological liar whose singular redeeming quality is his sheer physical radiance.
The collection of poetry, which won her the T.S. Eliot Prize, is dedicated to the English Romantic poet John Keats, challenging his famous aphorism, "Beauty is truth."

articles.title: Is it better to buy or rent?

blocks.text: Buyers or renters: Who ends up richer?

Buying a property is the largest purchase most Canadians will make in their lifetime. For many, it’s also their biggest investment. But strictly financially speaking, are you better off putting down a large down payment and facing higher monthly costs as an owner, or remaining a renter and investing your savings somewhere else? Who ends up with more money in their pocket at the end of the day?
Don't miss our simulator below. Keep reading to understand how to use it.

To answer this question, we analyzed over two decades of historical data on property prices, rents, inflation and interest rates across 22 Canadian metropolitan areas, alongside long-term stock market returns.

Using this data, we built an interactive simulator. Every time it runs, it calculates the monthly expenses and financial gains for three distinct paths: an owner with a fixed-rate mortgage, one with a variable-rate mortgage and a renter. Whenever the renter's monthly costs are lower than the homeowner's, those savings are automatically invested in stocks and bonds to compound over time.

The simulator projects these financial paths over a 25-year period across 1,000 unique scenarios. Some scenarios feature high rents and low interest rates; others simulate average inflation paired with weak stock market returns.

The calculations factor in mortgage payments, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, condo fees, rent and eventual selling fees. Every outcome represents a possible future based on historical patterns and the options you select.

Of course, no one can predict the future. This tool provides probabilities, not guarantees, and should not be used for major financial decisions. Below is a simplified version of our simulator. You can find a more comprehensive version with expanded options and a detailed methodology breakdown at the end of this article.
Home prices decline, while stocks surge

Our simulator is not perfect. The past is no guarantee of the future, and many macroeconomic factors are bound to change. Canada’s population is aging, the immigration outlook remains uncertain, an AI bubble could crash stock markets and countless variables continuously reshape the broader economy and housing markets.

Because comprehensive historical data is limited, our tool is based on the last 25 years, meaning it does not account for Canada's last major housing crash in the early 1990s. Several experts also pointed out that the cost of maintaining a property is often higher than estimated, especially when a roof starts to leak unexpectedly. Furthermore, realistically, few Canadians stay in the exact same home for a quarter-century.
A sandwich board is shown on a street on Quebec's unofficial moving day in Montreal on July 1. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)
Still, home prices have been declining over the last few years, while interest rates, average property taxes and maintenance costs have increased.
Meanwhile, the stock market has been surging. An investment made in 2005 would be worth roughly seven times more today, compared to just three times more for a property bought at the same time.

Based on this, our calculations reveal a clear trend: If you rent an average studio or one-bedroom apartment and aggressively invest the cash you save by not owning a condo, you have a strong chance of pulling ahead.
But as soon as you step up to a two-bedroom apartment or larger, that math changes quickly. Rent prices swallow up the surplus, making it nearly impossible to save and invest meaningfully.

In fact, in many scenarios, the monthly cost of renting eventually eclipses the cost of owning. A homeowner's largest monthly expense is their mortgage, typically locked in for a five-year term. Adjusted for inflation, the real value of that payment actually decreases over time.

items: Average asking rents fall 4.8% in August as trade war adds fresh uncertainty: report
Why N.S. rents are still increasing far faster than we saw historically for decades

blocks.text: Rents, on the other hand, almost always rise, often outpacing general inflation. Eventually, the lines cross. The renter begins paying more per month than the owner, wiping out their monthly savings and halting any new investment contributions.

Location, of course, dictates everything. In some regions, owning a condo loses the least amount of money after all cumulative expenses, compared to renting a two bedroom or bigger. Buying and then selling a condo is not a guaranteed profit. Single-family houses or townhouses offer a higher probability of financial return, but they come with a much steeper upfront purchase price.
'2 housing crises in Canada'

Yet for millions of Canadians, this debate is purely theoretical, and renting is their only option. Half of all couples in the cities we analyzed do not earn enough to qualify for an average condo in the city they live in — a figure that jumps to two-thirds for a house.
The outlook is even starker for the growing demographic of single-income households. Most Canadians are forced to rent, even when doing so is the less financially advantageous path.
“I would argue there are two housing crises in Canada,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“One is the housing crisis for the middle class, affording a condo in places like Toronto, Vancouver and increasingly in Montreal, especially since the pandemic. But there's an affordability crisis as well for low-income Canadians, who really need help just finding a place to live.”

Affordability is one factor causing younger generations to live with their parents for longer, a May 2026 Statistics Canada study found. They also tend to settle on a career, form a family and buy property later in life, a phenomenon described as “life-stretching.” And when they do finally leave the family nest, they also typically live alone or with roommates more often than previous generations.
This purchasing delay observed among younger Canadian generations can have massive compounding consequences.

“Timing is everything,” said Jean-Philippe Deschamps-Laporte, assistant director of the Centre for Housing and Income Statistics at Statistics Canada, who was involved with the report. When younger generations buy their first property later in their life compared to their parents, this investment has less time to potentially bear fruit.

items: Moving Back in with Parents & Coupons
How Nova Scotia became one of Canada's most expensive rental markets

blocks.text: “Younger generations could face returns that are not what they would have had if they had been born earlier."

His own research has found that when people graduate during a recession, it carries consequences for the rest of their lives. The same logic applies to the housing and stock markets. If you are lucky, you buy when prices are low and sell when they are high. But more often than not, you do not really get to choose, he notes, as it depends entirely on your current life stage.
So, should you buy or should you rent?

“The calculations done here are very useful for a lot of Canadians, but the most important thing is to do some introspection on how much owning a home will actually improve your life,” said James Macek, assistant professor at the University of Alberta's School of Business.
Kiana Basiri, assistant professor at the Toronto Metropolitan University, had a similar sentiment.
“We are kind of pushing people toward ownership at the expense of them being tighter financially and less resilient, simply because they really want to own something," she said.
"We just assume ownership is the best way for people to accumulate wealth over time, but I feel we need more education for people on how they can invest their savings in different ways.”
Furthermore, when people move to the suburbs to find more affordable properties, they sometimes forget to factor in other costs, like maintaining two cars instead of paying for public transit.
Fact check: Canadian real estate listings use AI-generated images

As Jean-Pierre Lessard, an economist and partner at Aviseo Conseil, put it: “We are crazy about property ownership in Canada, but there is no link between a nation's economic growth and its homeownership rate.”

A key point he made during a talk in a May 2026 conference was that it’s possible for the average household in Quebec City and Montreal to build more wealth by remaining renters instead of becoming owners.

items: Regina seniors, NDP call for rent control after increases at private retirement community
Toronto board of trade urges province to reform housing regulations

blocks.text: “Originally, public policies to encourage buying were intended to stimulate construction. We've lost sight of that,” Lessard said. “We need to return to something more rational.”

In some nations, it is entirely normal to be a lifelong renter. Germany and Switzerland, for example, are famous for having populations where more than half of all residents rent, backed by robust regulations that cap rent increases and protect tenants' rights.

“Overall, we need to increase the supply of both homeownership and rental units quite significantly,” said ab Iorwerth. The challenge, he said, is to balance supply with measures that encourage homeownership, such as the first home savings account, which tend to push prices up, while simultaneously ensuring there is enough inventory to keep homes affordable.

In June 2025, the CMHC published a report projecting that around 250,000 new housing units would be started each year over the next decade, whereas twice as many are actually needed to restore affordability.
Methodology

The detailed data sets and calculations used can be found here. Our methodology was shared prior to publication with the experts quoted in the article above, and their suggestions helped inform the analysis.
