articles.title: EU envoy in Beijing for talks to calm trade tensions
articles.summary: The EU trade envoy said he hoped to make progress in tackling the bloc's "unsustainable" trade imbalance with China. Beijing called for trade disputes to be resolved through equal dialogue.

image.caption: Maros Sefcovic said he hoped the discussions in China would yield tangible resultsImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP

blocks.text: EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic arrived in Beijing on Thursday for two days of talks on addressing the bloc's trade deficit with China.
"We're working hard to rebalance EU-China trade," Sefcovic wrote on X following a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in the Chinese capital.
Sefcovic added that it was "crucial" the talks deliver tangible outcomes.
Sefcovic said his visit, which lasts until Friday, aimed to tackle the "unsustainable" trade deficit, which is at its highest level since 2022, according to EU figures.

China exports around €1 billion ($1.12 billion) more in goods and services a day to the EU than flows the other way. Many in Europe blame this on unfair trade practices by Beijing, including using state subsidies and price dumping to undercut European rivals.
Beijing has rejected those claims.
China appeals for dialogue to solve disputes
Thursday's meeting comes after three months of discussions between EU and Chinese officials over the trade imbalance. Sefcovic has previously said he wanted to see results by October.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry on Thursday called for openness and cooperation, saying that "resolving economic and trade differences through equal dialogue and consultation is in the common interests of both China and the EU."
"We hope that the European side can work towards solutions together with China," ministry ​spokesperson Mao Ning said at a news briefing.
Earlier Thursday, Sefcovic met with representatives from EU companies in China.
"The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security," he said.

Besides the trade deficit, Sefcovic's discussions in China are also set to focus on an ongoing dispute over hybrid cars. According to diplomats, China has rejected calls to voluntarily limit its fast-rising export of the vehicles to the bloc.
Brussels could move to temporarily curb the import of Chinese cars through quotas and tariffs, something Beijing firmly opposes.
Merz, Macron call for new measures

Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for tougher EU measures to tackle unfair trade practices, which they said were undermining European companies and increasing the bloc's economic dependencies.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the current trade imbalance "leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe."
EU leaders are expected to discuss the bloc's relations with China at a summit in Brussels next week.

articles.title: India faces water and power shortages after weak monsoon
articles.summary: A weak monsoon in India is hitting farmers, water supplies and the power system, while raising wider questions about increasingly erratic rainfall and the economic costs.

image.caption: The economic impact of a poor monsoon can extend well beyond agricultureImage: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: Ramesh Reddy, 44, put everything he had into his 3.5 acre tomato farm in June. The farmer from Kolar district in the south of the state of Karnataka invested 320,000 rupees (€3,000, $3,357), borrowing 250,000 rupees at 24% annual interest and pledging his wife's wedding jewelry as collateral.

The harvest was meant to repay the loan and cover his son's overdue college fees. But then the farm's irrigation well ran dry. Within three weeks, the tomato plants had turned brown and Reddy could not salvage a single crate.
"I have lost everything I invested," he told DW. "I have no money left for the next crop and I don't know how I will repay the loan."
He is now negotiating a job as a security guard in the state capital, Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farmland behind.
Driest monsoon in 11 years
ForIndia, the monsoon is more than just a four-month rainy season. It replenishes reservoirs, supports agriculture and helps sustain water supplies and power generation across much of the country.
Nearly half of India's workforce depends on farming for their livelihood, doing jobs that are both tough and economically insecure.

This year, the country received 759.4 millimeters (ca. 30 inches) of rain between June and September, against a long-term average of 868.6 millimeters. The 12.6% deficit made it the country's driest monsoon in 11 years and the fourth driest this century.

blocks.caption: The monsoon replenishes reservoirs, supports agriculture and helps sustain water supplies and power generation across much of IndiaImage: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Indian Ministry of Earth Sciences, said the main factor behind the poor monsoon was a severe El Nino. He had warned earlier that this global climate phenomenon would posed a serious risk to rainfall.
"As far as the Indian monsoon is concerned, El Nino is the most important influencing factor, which we should consider very seriously,” Rajeevan told DW.
Water and power under pressure

The effects are now hitting India's water and energy systems. The country's major reservoirs ended the monsoon with less water than usual, leaving both farmers and the power sector with less of a buffer going into the months ahead.
Combined storage in the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission stood at 132.7 billion cubic meters, below the 10-year average of 151.1 billion cubic meters.

That shortfall is already being felt in electricity generation. Hydropower output fell nearly 16% in September from a year earlier, according to Grid India data. At the same time, electricity shortages reached 560 million kilowatt-hours, the highest monthly shortfall in more than three years. After sunset, when solar generation drops off, the grid has fewer options to make up the difference.

Coal-fired plants have, therefore, had to shoulder more of the load, but they face a problem of their own. Data from the Central Electricity Authority showed that around 40% of coal-fired plants had critically low stocks, with supplies below a quarter of the required level.
The government has ordered some private industrial power plants to operate at full capacity and feed surplus electricity into the grid.

Manufacturers are already feeling the strain. "Uninterrupted power supply is of paramount importance for manufacturing units, as power cuts disrupt production cycles," said Ashok Gupta, the president of the Mohali Industries Association, which represents nearly 600 small and medium-sized manufacturers.
"Such disruptions not only cause losses to manufacturers but also result in wastage of raw materials."
Urban farming for a new generation in Delhi
A hit to rural incomes

The economic impact of a poor monsoon can extend well beyond agriculture. Weaker farm output can hit rural incomes, employment and consumption, while higher food prices put further pressure on household budgets.

Arun Kumar, a retired professor of economics, said the effects could be wider than the headline economic numbers suggest, particularly because much of India's rural economy operates outside the formal sector.

"Economic development needs to be assessed through a wider set of indicators," Kumar told DW. He said weaker agricultural output could push up food prices while putting pressure on incomes and consumption.
Himanshu, a development economist at Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University, described the situation as a "twin shock" for rural households, with weaker farm incomes coming alongside higher food prices.
"When agricultural incomes fall and food prices rise, rural households face a squeeze on their purchasing power," he told DW.

The economist said that the uneven distribution of rainfall could compound the problem, with some farming regions suffering much heavier losses than the national rainfall figure indicates. "The impact on rural consumption could also be significant, as households facing lower incomes and higher food costs have less money to spend on other goods and services."
Outlook increasingly difficult to predict as climate warms

The pressure is also being felt in urban households. A survey in September by India's central bank found that households were expecting inflation to rise as food and fuel prices increasingly affected sentiment.
How vegetable gardens feed communities and minds
Sunita Sharma, a homemaker in New Delhi, said her usual shopping list now costs hundreds of rupees more than it did a few months ago.
"We have no option but to cut down on discretionary expenses just to afford basic, everyday meals," she told DW.

The prices of some staples have risen sharply recently. An analysis by ISignal using Department of Consumer Affairs data found that onions were 93% more expensive in September than a year earlier, while sugar prices rose by 28% and rice by about 8%.

The next test will be the rabi, or winter, crop. Farmers are now preparing to plant wheat, mustard and chickpeas, but success will depend largely on how much moisture remains in the soil after the weak monsoon.
Rajeevan said the longer-term outlook was also becoming increasingly difficult to predict as the climate warms.

"In a warming climate, longer dry spells and greater rainfall variability is a possibility," he said. "In future, in addition to the influence of El Nino events, we should expect the influence of a warmer climate."
Reddy, the farmer in Karnataka state, is now waiting to hear whether he has got the security job in Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farm behind.

articles.title: Marcos calls for culture shift to help fight corruption
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Thursday said that the Philippines needs to undergo a cultural shift amid the series of high-profile flood control corruption cases that rocked the nation.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 10:37pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Thursday said that the Philippines needs to undergo a cultural shift amid the series of high-profile flood control corruption cases that rocked the nation.
In a "24 Oras" report from Jonathan Andal, Marcos said that to address these issues of corruption, the changes needed to go beyond the bureaucratic.

“When you are a second-class citizen for 300-plus years, you find ways to get around the law. Because you cannot succeed if you just follow the law. Now we have to change that…However, again, a cultural shift is much, much harder than what you say a bureaucratic shift or a systems change…It's not an easy job. But it is something we absolutely have to do,” Marcos said during the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore.
Corruption needed to become unacceptable, said the President.

The multi-billion flood control scam was allegedly a systemic kickback scheme between lawmakers and contractors, wherein public funds were funneled into substandard or ghost infrastructure projects. The scam contributed to the Philippines’ economic slump.
Pax Silica

During the conference, Marcos was also asked about the controversial Pax Silica project. The president said that he was excited for the initiative, encouraging business leaders in the audience to invest in the Philippines.

“That is one of the big areas that we're terribly excited about. Pax Silica came along and we saw that it was a grand opportunity for the Philippines to inhabit more of the value chain that we already had begun,” Marcos said.
The President said that by November, the Digital Economy Framework Agreement will be finalized, which will act as the country’s guide to the use of artificial intelligence (AI).
Addressing the business leaders at the forum, Marcos touted the country’s young workforce and the country’s relaxed rules for foreign investors.
For example, foreigners are now allowed full ownership of corporations in select industries, including technology.
Marcos is in Singapore for a working visit until September 11. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife indicted for alleged torture of US citizens
articles.summary:
Ousted Venezuelan president and Cilia Flores have been in jail in New York since early January

The deposed Venezuelan president

blocks.text: The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.

The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pre-trial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been held in a New York City jail since early January.

They were captured in a US military operation and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism” charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them.
CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.
The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly used horrific tactics to suppress opposition and maintain their control.

They presided “over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the charging document said.

“That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims’ families, including children,” it added.
Maduro and Flores, the new indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”.

Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.
The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.
after newsletter promotion

“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”

Amid news of this new indictment, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.
Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.
“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”
Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.
Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lb and lost two teeth since her detention.

“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest.

The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. They argued in court and legal filings that Flores presented an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public”. Prosecutors also insisted that she had received adequate medical care.

Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid to Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
articles.summary: Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.

blocks.text: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.
The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".

Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.
The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.
"She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said.
"She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."

articles.title: World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?
articles.summary: Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this…

image.caption: Neom Stadium, one of the planned stadiums for the 2034 World Cup, is likely not being builtImage: Balkis Press/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111miles) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.
Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general re-evaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing. The draw-back from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."
Priorities changing, with sports losing out

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multi-billion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.
How the Iran war has ruined Saudi Arabia's 'Vision 2030'

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.
Parallels between Qatar 2022 and Saudi Arabia 2034

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry nor FIFA have responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.
"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a Fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.
"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames."

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia will host its first World Cup in 2034 but has been a regular at the tournamentImage: Saudi Arabia Football Association/Handout via REUTERS

blocks.text: Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."
World Cup will still matter to Saudi Arabia
But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.
"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."
Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.
Gulf Cup hosting a postivie sign before Asian Cup test

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.
Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions.”

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.

articles.title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
articles.summary: Bernadette Greene-Placentia says her memory of the attack is spotty and that she was knocked unconscious.

blocks.text: A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times, external she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her.
She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later.
Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place".
"No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office.
Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims.
The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans.
She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."
The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing.
After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event.
When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times.
Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination.
She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times.
She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain.

The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte fit for trial, says ICC
articles.summary: '[The chamber] is satisfied that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial,' says the International Criminal Court Trial…

blocks.text: DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.
Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool via Reuters

'[The chamber] is satisfied that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial,' says the International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court has cleared an obstacle in Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming November trial as the ICC Trial Chamber III found that the former Philippine president is fit for trial.

“For these reasons, the chamber is satisfied that the Expert Panel’s Reports are sufficiently conclusive to make a determination on the Accused’s ability to participate in the trial proceedings and to effectively exercise his procedural and fair trial rights,” the ICC Trial Chamber III said on Thursday, October 8.
“[The chamber] is satisfied that the Accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings and is therefore fit to stand trial,” it added.

Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity before the ICC due to the alleged killings of the Davao Death Squad and his war on drugs, which killed nearly 30,000 people according to several human rights groups.

In March 2025, the former president became the first Asian head of state to be arrested by the ICC over the same case. His trial is set to begin on November 30, following the ICC’s decision to confirm all the charges against him and the junking of his appeal on jurisdictional grounds.
Just last January, the ICC pre-trial chamber that handled the confirmation of charges found that the former president was able to stand trial. – Rappler.com

articles.title: House passes proposed P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget on 2nd reading
articles.summary: The House of Representatives passed on the second reading the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget--but not without any criticisms from several lawmakers.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 9:53pm
The House of Representatives passed on the second reading the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget—but not without any criticisms from several lawmakers.
In a 24 Oras report from Tina Panganiban-Perez on Thursday, the budget was passed with P116 billion in budget realignments. Several lawmakers questioned the budgetary changes.

ACT Teachers Partylist Representative Antonio Tinio questioned why there was not a detailed report by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee (BARSc) for its recommended changes to the proposed budget.
“Yung mga increases na pinropose sa BARSc ay mga lump sum increases lang. Hindi idinetalye kung saan mapupunta,” Tinio said.
(The increases proposed by the BARSc are mere lump sums. It is not detailed where it would go.)

However, House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin suspended the session to settle Tinio’s concern. According to the House leadership, the budget discussions were all livestreamed and the amendments were indicated in the proposed measure. All of the lawmakers were also given a copy and it is uploaded to the website.
“As such, the majority submits that the point of order is not well taken,” House Deputy Majority Leader Manuel Fortes said.
The People’s Budget Coalition also did not approve of the P199 billion that was moved around in the budget. One of these changes included added aid to the transport sector.

“Fuel subsidy to transport sector affected by rising fuel prices, the amount of P498.960 billion appropriated here shall be used to provide a nationwide fuel subsidy to duly licensed PUV's, taxis, tricycles, and ridehailing and service delivery vehicles,” Gabriela Women's Party Representative Sarah Elago said.
House appropriations Chair Mikaela Suansing defended this budget for transport aid.

“The amount in the NEP (National Expenditure Program) for the fuel subsidy to the transport sector is currently at zero, and the recommendation of the budget amendments review subcommittee is to add P1 billion to that,” Suansing said.
Meanwhile, Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco asked for a list of Department of Public Works and Highways projects that lawmakers were asking for.
“Mandatory publication of the House budget utilization and member-specific expenditures, under the special provisions of the House of Representatives,” Tiangco said.
Suansing replied and said that the Department of Budget and Management posts such projects on their website and the different district engineering offices could be searched.
There needs to be three days between the approval of a bill from the second reading to the third and final reading.
As a result, the House is expected to pass the budget on the third reading by Monday, October 12. — Jean Mangaluz/BM, GMA News

articles.title: Marcoleta's bail plea in plunder case deemed submitted for resolution
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division is set to decide whether or not it will allow Sen. Rodante Marcoleta and his co-accused to post bail in their plunder cases.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 9:52pm
The Sandiganbayan Third Division is set to decide whether or not it will allow Sen. Rodante Marcoleta and his co-accused to post bail in their plunder cases.
According to Maki Pulido's report on "24 Oras," the issue of Marcoleta’s bail has already been deemed submitted for resolution. The anti-graft court will issue a decision in the coming days.
In the Guidelines on Continuous Trial of Criminal Cases, the court has 30 days to resolve this, meaning that the court has to decide by November 19.

Marcoleta is currently detained in the New Quezon City Jail for his plunder case, which stemmed from the P75 million he admitted to receiving from former lawmaker Mike Defensor and businessmen Joseph Espiritu and Aristotle Viray. He reportedly received the amount while he was still a lawmaker in the House of Representatives.
While the court is resolving the matter, Marcoleta’s trial continues.
The first trial date was held on Thursday morning; the prosecution presented the evidence against Marcoleta and his three co-accused.

The evidence presented included a link to the television show where Marcoleta admitted to receiving the money as well as the verified position paper that Macroleta submitted to the Commission on Election where he admitted that the P75 million became a part of his personal funds and not a campaign donation.

The prosecution was meant to present as witnesses the lawyers who notarized the deed of donation for Defensor and the other co-accused, but Marcoleta’s camp moved to exempt them, citing attorney-client privilege.
Both sides agreed that the documents were authentic.
Marcoleta’s counsel is expected to present evidence for his defense on October 19. —Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Giorgia Meloni wins vote on controversial ‘bonus seat’ changes to electoral system
articles.summary: Italy’s opposition parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that rewarding those with 42% of support distorts public representation

blocks.text: A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.

Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.
The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.
There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.

Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.

Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.

Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy, had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.

While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.

Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.

Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party, said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

articles.title: Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention
articles.summary: Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, but Chile and Brazil have seen the fastest growth, especially with bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

image.caption: In Brazil, rates of bowel cancer in people under 50 years increased by 7.6% per year from 2000 to 2023Image: Samunella/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases through better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.

Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 years in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice the number what it was at the turn of the century.

That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the US and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.
So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in London.
"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."
But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.
A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.
In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.

In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in São Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.
The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.
But since the figures come from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.
"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."

Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.
These six cancers affect young adults most
In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.
Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — rose among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.

In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.

This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.
Better awareness could explain the rise in diagnoses
A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.
Death rates remained unchanged.

The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.

But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.
Bowel cancer rates rising in young people
The link between cancer and obesity
Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).
According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.
Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.
What you consume matters:

items: Processed meat is classed as carcinogenic
Alcohol is also considered a risk factor
Fiber (vegetables, whole grains and pulses) lowers cancer risk

blocks.text: Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.
"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."
How young people can lower their cancer risk
Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needs public health policy.
But he also said young people can lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.
"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."
For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.

articles.title: Germany news: UK's Burnham visits Berlin for talks with Merz
articles.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is visiting Berlin to launch a new bilateral treaty and hold talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. President Steinmeier is on a state visit to France. DW has more.
articles.byline: Mark Hallam, Emilio Reynoso, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Burnham was greeted with military honors in BerlinImage: Carsten Koall/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 8, 2026
Merz, Burnham inaugurate new German-British friendship treaty

blocks.caption: Burnham was welcomed with military honors in Berlin on ThursdayImage: Carsten Koall/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz received relatively new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham with military honors in Berlin.
During Burnham's visit, the new Treaty on Friendship and Bilateral Cooperation between the UK and Germany — signed last year by previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer — officially comes into force.
Aslo known as the Kensington Treaty, the 27-page document lays out a 17-point action plan for closer cooperation in the post-Brexit era, with the UK no longer a part of the EU.
Merz called it a historic day and said the deal opened up new opportunities for bilateral cooperation, particularly for students and young people.

"That's what we're doing this for," Merz said. "So that the young generation also notices when it comes to bilateral relations between Germany as part of the EU and the UK, how well we Europeans work together and how much we belong together, too."

blocks.caption: Merz and Burnham ushered in the Kensington Treaty in the presence of a young audienceImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Burnham said that the Kensington Treaty would improve security in Europe, help both economies grow and improve people's living standards.

"In challenging times, and these are challenging times, we need the strongest possible cooperation with our closest partners and Germany really is one of our closest partners," the former mayor of Manchester said.
Burnham also said that he was open to Germany joining the GCAP program, a partnership between Britain, Italy and Japan to build a next-generation multirole combat aircraft.

"I've indicated to the chancellor ... our openness to Germany joining GCAP," he said at a press conference. "That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan."

blocks.caption: Merz and Burnham had one-on-one talks in the chancellery during the visitImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A rival Franco-German plan to build a next-generation military jet, FCAS, collapsed in June.

The GCAP project has been set up to allow for different levels of involvement. It expanded in July when Canada signed up as an observer, and Saudi Arabia had also been touted as a potential interested party.
Germany already works with the UK and Italy on the joint Eurofighter Typhoon project.
Italy and Japan would need to join Burnham in indicating a willingness for Germany participating in this project.

articles.title: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
articles.summary: Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani had been secretly released on parole in 2025, after serving less than half his sentence.
articles.byline: Endang Nurdin and Rebecca Henschke, BBC News Indonesia

blocks.text: A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.

Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.

A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.
On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.
"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.
The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.
But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.
That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.
Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".
"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.
For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.
"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.
Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.
"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.
She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.

She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".

articles.title: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the move will deliver more stable government, but opposition parties say her aim is to stay in power.

blocks.text: Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.

The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A coalition or party winning more than 42% of the vote will be awarded dozens of additional seats in parliament - which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.

articles.title: Bear kills man in home attack near Mongolian capital
articles.summary: Police say the bear entered a traditional nomadic dwelling near Ulaanbaatar, killing a man and seriously injured a woman.

blocks.text: A bear has killed a man and seriously injured a woman after it attacked them in their home near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar.
Police say the incident happened in the Bayanzurkh district overnight on Wednesday in their traditional Mongolian nomadic tent-like structure known as a ger.

The man, who was in his 40s, died, but the woman, in her 50s, managed to flee and raise the alarm with neighbours. She is in a serious condition in hospital, city official Munkhbayar M told reporters.
Sightings of bears around humans are becoming more common in Mongolia, for reasons that include climate change and food scarcity.
A team of rangers is searching for the bear while officials have warned locals to be vigilant and report any sightings.
There had been 24 bear sightings near the capital this year alone, compared to just two in 2018, Munkhbayar said, in comments reported by the AFP news agency.

Videos showing bears entering or damaging gers, and attacking livestock have reportedly gone viral on Mongolian social media in recent weeks, highlighting the increase in bear and human interaction across the country.
Bear-hunting permits across eight provinces have been issued and officials are seeking to obtain tranquiliser dart guns to support rangers in rural areas, AFP reports.
A significant amount of Mongolians are nomadic, but settled agricultural communities are becoming more common. An increasing number of the population lives in the capital or other major urban areas.

articles.title: Security in the Black Sea region: is Bulgaria the weak link in Europe's defense against threats from Russia?
articles.summary: Two ships have sunk off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania after drone attacks in recent days. Sofia has held back on pointing the finger at Russia. What does that mean for security in the Black Sea…

image.caption: A Bulgarian border police vessel carries crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack on TuesdayImage: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Although security in the Baltic Sea and the threat of Russian provocation there are the subject of regular public debate, security in the Black Sea is a subject that sometimes gets less attention in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine even though the Black Sea is to a degree an active frontline in the war.
There are multiple reasons why the Black Sea's security is such a complex issue, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is.
On October 6, two cargo ships — the Alfa Watan and the Able — were struck by drones in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning.
The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna.

blocks.caption: Crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel on TuesdayImage: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS

blocks.text: The day before, another cargo ship — the Royad Mammadov — was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania. Two crew members lost their lives.
Multiple recent attacks on ships
These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine.
As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe.

"Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab.
PM downplays drone attacks

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident."
Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia.
After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place.
Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand."
Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end."

blocks.caption: Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev said that there is no concrete evidence that Russia was behind the attackImage: Spasiyana Sergieva/REUTERS

blocks.text: The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration.
Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense?

For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China.
"This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW.

"The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said.

According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation.
No smoking gun
One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain.

blocks.caption: The cargo vessel Able (pictured here in Istanbul, Turkey, on an unknown date), which was carrying Ukrainian grain, was damaged when hit by a drone on October 6Image: Tony Hogwood/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ruslan Trad says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof.

"The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities."

Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice."
Economic consequences
A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5, which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected.

blocks.caption: A marine drone, which Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said was destroyed by F-16 fighter jets in AugustImage: Radu Miruta via Facebook/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov.
Nevertheless, Ruslan Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine.
"This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said.

"The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added.
Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara, this is not enough.

She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said.
Turkey's leverage and China's role

Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea.

blocks.caption: Another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania on October 5. Pictured here: Firefighters and rescue workers wait to help the survivorsImage: Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.

"A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said.
Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole.

In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently.
Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor.

"We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China, which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region."

articles.title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026
articles.summary:
World’s most prestigious prize for literature goes to Canadian poet known for genre-crossing works including Autobiography of Red

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the…

blocks.text: The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Born in 1950 in Toronto, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986, and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.

Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.

Her work has attracted praise from fellow writers, including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”

Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera. Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avante-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

articles.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
articles.summary: Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

image.caption: A huge underwater oil project could transform the Falkland Islands' economy, but it is also fueling a longstanding sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UKImage: Martin Zwick/Danita Delimont/IMAGO

blocks.text: Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.
However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.
A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Rally around the flag?

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."
He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.
"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

blocks.caption: Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falkand Islands' Legislative AssemblyImage: Legislative Assembly of the Falkland Islands

blocks.text: Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."
Potentially transformative for the Falklands
Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."
However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

blocks.caption: Argentina's President Javier Milei says he is taking legal action against the Sea Lion oilfield projectImage: Argentina's Presidency Press Office/AFP

blocks.text: Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.
"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.
However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.
"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."
More economic pressure from Argentina

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

blocks.caption: The project could transform the Falklands' small economyImage: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.
While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.
"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

articles.title: Residents airlifted to safety after flooding in central Chile
articles.summary: The Mapocho river has burst its banks after an unusually large amount of rain fell in recent days.

blocks.text: Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.
Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.
Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.

They have warned that this year's unusually strong El Niño climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.
Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death.
In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.
Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.
