articles.title: Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
articles.summary: Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her deep reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

image.caption: Anne Carson has been touted amongst the favorites to win the prize for several years [FILE: 2015]Image: Pontus Lundahl/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."
Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.

The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.
What is Anne Carson known for?
Born in Toronto in 1950, her family moved around many small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.

Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regard translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.

Carson is also highly influenced by the King James Bible, as well as more modern writers like Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov award.

Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did reveal in 2024 that she suffers from Parkinson's disease.
Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?

items: The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, which makes it possible to study how the brain works.
The Nobel Prize in physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demistify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.
The Nobel Prize in chemistry went to Henri B. Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan on Wednesday, for solving the longstanding mystery of homochirality in living organisms.

blocks.text: What happens next?

The winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. They are also given a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, where they are expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.
On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, following by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine ambassador amid POW dispute
articles.summary: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine. Seoul is upset about a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war being made public knowledge at the UN and had demanded — but not…

image.caption: The dispute can trace its roots back to President Zelenskyy's speech at the UN General Assembly last month [FILE: September 23, 2026]Image: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea said on Thursday that it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a deepening diplomatic rift over making the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul public last month.

The two countries have been at loggerheads since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's speech at the UN General Assembly, during which he spoke about the capture and later the transfer of two North Korean soldiers who had been fighting against Ukraine alongside Russian forces.
South Korea has called for an apology from Ukraine, saying the comments breached a confidentiality agreement and could put the POWs' families still in North Korea at risk.
Kyiv, meanwhile, has said no such agreement existed and voiced a desire to smooth over a "diplomatic understanding," but stopped short of apologizing.

blocks.caption: A South Korean lawmaker, Yu Yong-weon, had visited the POWs at a camp in Ukraine after their captureImage: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did South Korea's Foreign Ministry say about recalling its ambassador?
"The govenment has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine," Seoul's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday.
"The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and wil continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end," it said.

blocks.caption: North Korea's Kim Jong Un has posed prominently with wounded soldiers who were deployed to assist Russian in its war against UkraineImage: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: Last week, President Lee Jae Myung called for a "public apology" from Kyiv and said South Korea would take "additional measures" if one was not forthcoming. He said that during the prisoner swap, "the Ukrainian side demanded confidentiality and agreed to it, but unilaterally disclosed it."

When challenged with what Myung described as "utmost courtesy," he said Kyiv instead denied the existence of a confidentiality agreement, making him out to be a liar, and spoke of the prospect of war on the Korean peninsula.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, had spoken of a "diplomatic misunderstanding" that he said "we sincerely hope to resolve."
Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy

Bilateral tensions also emerged this week amid the publication of an investigative report in The Guardian claiming that fuel was being shipped to Russia from South Korea via sanctioned tankers, alleviating the strains on diesel supplies amid Ukraine targeting Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure.

South Korea has walked a fine line on Russia's war in Ukraine, providing humanitarian and non-lethal equipment to Kyiv, as well as financial assistance, but also seeking to maintain cordial ties with Russia, which has a small land border with North Korea near Vladivostock.

North Korea, meanwhile, sent troops to help Russia reclaim the border region of Kursk that Ukraine was able to partially occupy, and has since celebrated this deployment at home with much fanfare, while seeking closer ties to Putin's Russia.

blocks.caption: North Korea has elected to use the deployment in Russia as a tool for domestic propaganda and diplomatic relations rather than to keep it quietImage: KCNA/REUTERS

articles.title: As Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian data centers, could Ukraine soon be offline?
articles.summary: As Russia targets Ukraine's data centers more and more, experts say the country's internet system is too robust to shut down entirely. However, services could become more expensive.

image.caption: Data centers are essential for maintaining online servicesImage: Serjunco/Westend61/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs.
Since early September, Russia has been targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically.

Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting.
Why is Russia targeting Ukrainian data centers?

The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly.

Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians."
Has Russia changed its approach in its war with Ukraine?
Could Ukraine go offline?

Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks, experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized.

"The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services."

He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world."
At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly.
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats

Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook.
How can data and devices be protected?

Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained.
He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon.
What happens when data centers lose power?

Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained.

Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers.
"We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change."
Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Russian strike on buses kills 33, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
articles.summary: Ukraine accused Russia of targeting the crowded bus in the frontline city to kill as many civilians as possible.

blocks.text: Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting a bus carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
However, Thursday's attack follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.

Russia is now launching constant air raids against Ukraine, with sirens ringing throughout the day in the capital Kyiv. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.

In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack, however rescue officials said the attack caused a fire on two buses that were both carrying passengers.
Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the Donetsk region to move to safer regions of Ukraine.

Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.

Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.

Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".

Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the best defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.

For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.

Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets."

articles.title: Russian attack on two buses kills 30 near Ukraine frontline
articles.summary: Authorities say 18 people also wounded after incident in Kramatorsk in country’s ‘fortess belt’

blocks.text: Thirty people have been killed after Russia struck two passenger buses in Kramatorsk, near the frontline in eastern Ukraine, according to local authorities.

“As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack on buses has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office said. The governor’s office gave the same toll and said public transport had been suspended.
Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus.

“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said ‌on the Telegram app. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”

Moscow’s forces have stepped ​up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt“, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk ⁠region.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the region still under its ​control before it stops fighting, which ​Kyiv refuses to ‌do.
Thursday’s attack ​came ​a day after dozens were killed in a Russian air strikes across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid.
More details soon …

articles.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.summary: Casualties have been reported on the vessel, identified by a maritime intelligence firm as the oil and chemical tanker, Acers.

blocks.text: A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal and there were casualties reported, the UKMTO said.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers, which was reported as laden with cargo on Saturday as it sailed towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).

The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.

Vanguard also reported a fire on board another tanker on Thursday in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. It said the vessel was likely to be the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The cause of the fire is unclear and the UKMTO has not reported an incident in the area.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.

blocks.text: South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.

But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.

In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.

This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.

Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Christa Pike now walking after US execution went wrong, lawyer tells BBC
articles.summary: A lawyer says the murderer of Colleen Slemmer is moving around her hospital room after surviving two lethal injections.

blocks.text: Christa Pike is "up and walking" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.

Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally "foggy".
Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

In their updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had previously said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.

In the latest updates, given to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital, which was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September.
Once it became clear that Pike was not going to die, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to have be in a critical condition.
As of late on Tuesday, though, she was "fairly well", Ferrell told the BBC.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, he added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."

Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".

Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.

Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.

For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.

The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

articles.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
articles.summary: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

blocks.text: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside and several staff were seen entering on Thursday morning.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.
In a written statement on the morning of the deadline, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK does not accept Israel has the right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.
However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

articles.title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary says former consulate general will remain independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people

The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general…

blocks.text: The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​will not be closing but will ⁠be known as a UK mission, remaining independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people.
Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to close ‌on Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank.
Miliband said that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks, it would now work to build up its presence.
He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, ‌following speculation it ​could expel some Israeli diplomats from Britain.

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians.

Israel had threatened to close it in protest at the UK’s decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused the governing Labour party of being hostile towards his country.

The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.

The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
after newsletter promotion

Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believes this is a matter for international courts to determine.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
articles.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

blocks.text: The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Palestinians in Gaza face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
articles.summary: Many Palestinians are still living in cramped tent cities, with the US plan to end the war largely stalled.

blocks.text: In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.

She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.

"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.

The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.

His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.

Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.

"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.

Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."
Additional reporting by Imogen Anderson and Malak Hassouneh

articles.title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
articles.summary: Bassam al-Hassan, linked to reporter Austin Tice's abduction, is being sheltered in return for information.

blocks.text: A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity, external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.

Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.

An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.
Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command.

Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.

We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.

In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.
"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."

As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.

Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.

Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.
Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.

One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".
Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.

The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.

Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.

There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.
Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.

They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".

Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

articles.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
articles.summary:
Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases

South Korea will take legal action if it finds…

blocks.text: South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.

The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”

Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.

Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.

The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.

The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.

The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.

On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
articles.summary:
Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest…

blocks.text: Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.

Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.

The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.

Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.

Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%

The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

articles.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
articles.summary:
NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class…
articles.byline: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies

blocks.text: The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.

The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.

“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.

Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.

The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.

The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.

Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
articles.summary: Known for his intense performances, Patekar carved out a distinctive place in Indian cinema.

blocks.text: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances and distinct dialogue delivery, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told the BBC.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters in films such as Parinda, Krantiveer and Ab Tak Chhappan. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.
He was rushed to hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.
"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. His portrayal of the volatile, gritty gangster Anna won him his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award.

He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. Then there was the villainous character of Majid Khan in Angaar, the patriotic firebrand of Tirangaa, and, most notably, Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, for which he won the national award for best actor.
Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.
Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.

The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the depth of his talent. He has played gangsters, soldiers, policemen, politicians, patriots, villains, comic characters and tragic figures, while moving between Hindi and Marathi cinema and sometimes also working behind the camera as a director and writer.
His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a testament to his career.

Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before cinema made him a familiar face, he spent years working in theatre, where he developed the intensity and discipline that would become hallmarks of his screen performances.
Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.

articles.title: France's school protests: what lies behind the anger
articles.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.

The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.

"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France . Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.

There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.

The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.

Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.

And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

blocks.caption: Image caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.

Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.

To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.

In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
The street does not always win.

In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings

blocks.text: Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings

The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.

His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.

But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

articles.title: Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
articles.summary: Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections.

blocks.text: A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.
Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.
Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.

His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.
A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.

Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.
Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.
Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.
"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

articles.title: Trump wants a new Camp David retreat at his posh Florida golf club
articles.summary: Trump's estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David and mark another tradition transformed by Trump.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
President Trump gestures before boarding Marine One departs after a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on 31 July 2026 in Thurmont, Maryland.
ByBernd Debusmann and Sareen Habeshian
US President Donald Trump is looking to create a presidential retreat similar to Camp David at his Florida golf club.
The club would foot constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and provide free memberships to future presidents - and accommodations to visiting foreign dignitaries.
"It's only about two minutes away from the airport … and they could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like a sort of Camp David retreat," Trump said on Wednesday.

If it comes to fruition, Trump's transformed golf estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David, once a Great Depression-era camp in the woods for federal employees. It would also mark another tradition transformed by Trump.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A view of the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida.

blocks.text: A view of the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida.

The US president has sought to cement his legacy through changes to the White House, including gilded gold leaf accents in the Oval Office, demolition of the East Wing and construction of a ballroom. He is pushing ahead with plans to erect a massive triumphal arch elsewhere in Washington.

He has hosted national security meetings and other events at Camp David, known as the president's country residence. The Camp David property - set deep in Catoctin Mountain Park in Frederick County, Maryland - was first taken over as a retreat by President Franklin Roosevelt, who nicknamed it "Shangri-La".

The area is rustic, and in some ways resembles the military facility it officially is - Naval Support Facility, Thurmont. The entire facility is staffed by uniformed members of the US Navy and Marine Corps.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US President Joe Biden, center, greets Fumio Kishida, Japan's prime minister, right, and Yoon Suk Yeol, South Korea's president, left, during a trilateral summit at Camp David in 2023.

blocks.text: US President Joe Biden, center, greets Fumio Kishida, Japan's prime minister, right, and Yoon Suk Yeol, South Korea's president, left, during a trilateral summit at Camp David in 2023.

The secure facility is largely hidden from public view, with Marines guarding the perimeter and airspace above restricted. It is not marked on maps of the national park, even if its location is known to locals.
Press is only very rarely allowed on the grounds - meaning that photography of the wood and stone cabins and lodges that make up most of the facility are tightly controlled.

On a recent visit by the BBC, for example, reporters in the White House press pool were under strict instructions to avoid taking images in unauthorized areas or providing details on the camp's layout.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Then-US President Barack Obama (L) meets with Eurozone leaders on the Laurel Cabin patio during the G8 Summit on in 2012 at Camp David.

blocks.text: Then-US President Barack Obama (L) meets with Eurozone leaders on the Laurel Cabin patio during the G8 Summit on in 2012 at Camp David.

Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, on the other hand, is connected to the rest of the city by ample roadways, some of which are lined with supporters or protesters when the president is there.

The 27-hole golf course and club bills itself as having "a lively social scene" and fine dining - and is visited often by Trump's political allies during his many weekends in Florida. It includes a luxurious clubhouse, a gift store and hosts frequent social events for members.

The president's argument that the area is "secure" is notable. In recent months, Trump has frequently used national security and safety arguments to justify various projects in Washington DC, including his White House ballroom project the planned Triumphal Arch.

Asked by reporters if he would call the new presidential retreat at his golf club "Camp Donald", Trump replied, "Well, it's already called Trump International. It's one of the best golf courses in the world."
He said among advantages is the absence of high buildings and homes looming "so you don't have ... people hiding behind windows".
"They can get maximum safety," the president said. "It's a great idea and it'll be used a lot."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The entrance driveway at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County, Florida

blocks.text: The entrance driveway at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County, Florida
Trump said at the Oval Office on Wednesday that Secret Service officials first suggested the idea of using the golf club as a presidential retreat, and that he thinks it is "a great idea".
"It's about as safe as they could possibly get," he said.
The BBC has contacted the Secret Service for comment.

A letter dated 3 September from the golf course's attorney to the county commission in Florida said Trump offered to deem the club as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course" for presidents and visiting heads of state, according to USA TODAY's Palm Beach Post.
The letter, obtained by the local outlet, states that the golf club would provide access to all its facilities at "no cost to the federal government" and provide free membership to future presidents.
The golf club would front constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and local residents, according to the letter.
"This wouldn't be for me," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday. "This would be for all future presidents."

blocks.caption: Image caption, US President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking walk on grounds of presidential retreat Camp David in 2001.

blocks.text: US President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking walk on grounds of presidential retreat Camp David in 2001.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.
